```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo       = TRUE,
  message    = FALSE,
  warning    = FALSE,
  cache      = TRUE,
  cache.lazy = FALSE,   # model objects are large; lazy loading fails on them
  autodep    = TRUE,    # let knitr work out chunk dependencies from object usage
  comment    = "#>",
  fig.align  = "center",
  dpi        = 110
)
options(width = 110, scipen = 6)   # keep counts readable, but let tiny p-values
                                   # stay in scientific notation rather than print as 0

library(tidyverse)
library(survival)
library(broom)
library(coxme)
library(kableExtra)
library(here)      # portable paths anchored at the repo root (.Rproj / .git)

BASE <- here("data", "processed")   # repo-root/data/processed, wherever the repo lives

# The injury rulebook, so the classification helpers (injury_severity_ioc etc.) are
# the exact same ones the data was built with rather than a second copy.
source(here("analysis", "1. Injury Classification Rules.R"))

# Must match the value used when the panel was built in file 4.
RETURN_DURABILITY_GAMES <- 8

# One consistent table style for the whole document.
show_tbl <- function(x, caption = NULL, digits = 3) {
  kbl(x, caption = caption, digits = digits) %>%
    kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
                  full_width = FALSE, position = "left", font_size = 13)
}

# HR = exp(coef); returns NA if the term isn't in that model.
hr <- function(fit, term) {
  b <- coef(fit)[term]
  if (is.na(b)) NA_real_ else round(exp(b), 3)
}

# p-values here span 0.97 down to ~1e-11. Rounding to 3 dp would print the tiny
# ones as "0.000", which reads as "exactly zero" - so anything under 0.001 is
# shown in scientific notation instead.
fmt_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(is.na(p), NA_character_,
         ifelse(p < 0.001, formatC(p, format = "e", digits = 2),
                           formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)))
}
```

# Stage 0 - The modelling dataset {#stage0}

Feeds article 2.1, 2.3 and Table 1.

```{r load-data}
cox <- readRDS(file.path(BASE, "cox_ready_2021-26.rds"))

# The overuse tier is sub-divided the way Stage 6 reports it, so the reader meets the
# diagnosed / symptom-only counts here rather than for the first time in the results.
.named <- !cox$INJURY_TISSUE %in% c("non_specific", "not_recorded")
.n_diag  <- sum(cox$event_repetitive == 1 &  .named)
.n_sympt <- sum(cox$event_repetitive == 1 & !.named)
.n_unclass <- sum(cox$event) - sum(cox$event_repetitive) -
              sum(cox$event_acute_nc) - sum(cox$event_acute_imp)
f <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")

data_summary <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("Player-game intervals (rows)", "Distinct players", "Seasons",
               "New-injury events (primary outcome)",
               "  - overuse (repetitive mechanism)",
               "      of which: pathology named", "      of which: symptom only",
               "  - acute non-contact", "  - acute impact (negative control)",
               "  - mechanism not classifiable",
               "All-injury events (new + reaggravation)",
               "  - overuse (repetitive mechanism)", "  - acute non-contact",
               "  - acute impact (negative control)"),
  Value = c(
    f(nrow(cox)), f(n_distinct(cox$PLAYER_ID)),
    sprintf("%d (%s to %s)", n_distinct(cox$SEASON), min(cox$SEASON), max(cox$SEASON)),
    f(sum(cox$event)),
    f(sum(cox$event_repetitive)), f(.n_diag), f(.n_sympt),
    f(sum(cox$event_acute_nc)), f(sum(cox$event_acute_imp)), f(.n_unclass),
    f(sum(cox$event_recurrent)),
    f(sum(cox$event_repetitive_recurrent)),
    f(sum(cox$event_acute_nc_recurrent)),
    f(sum(cox$event_acute_imp_recurrent))
  )
)
show_tbl(data_summary, "The counting-process dataset")
```

Each row is one player-game interval `(t_start, t_stop]` with an event
indicator. The clock is game number within a season, and a player only
contributes rows while genuinely at risk: once an injury starts the
remaining missed games are removed, and they re-enter when they play
again.

`r format(sum(cox$event), big.mark = ",")` new-injury events across
`r format(n_distinct(cox$PLAYER_ID), big.mark = ",")` players. That is
large enough that p-values stop being informative on their own, so
throughout I read effect size first and significance second.

The mechanism tiers do not quite sum to that total: `r .n_unclass`
episodes carry no classifiable mechanism, because every report filed for
them was management text with no pathology in it. They stay in the
primary outcome, since they are genuine injuries, and drop out only of
the tier-specific models in Stage 6.

## How I classify injuries

Following the IOC consensus statement (Bahr et al. 2020), which
recommends recording body region, tissue type, mechanism and severity
independently rather than as one label. The NBA reports support this
better than I expected: they are written as
`Injury/Illness - <SITE>; <PATHOLOGY>`, so site and pathology are
already separate fields, and about nine in ten carry a side.

```{r injury-taxonomy}
ep <- cox %>% filter(IS_NEW_INJURY == 1 | IS_REAGGRAVATION == 1)

# A team's schedule density, so I can express the durability window in weeks.
team_games_per_week <- cox %>% distinct(SEASON, TEAM_ID, GAME_DATE) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, TEAM_ID) %>%
  summarise(g = n(), span = as.numeric(max(GAME_DATE) - min(GAME_DATE)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  summarise(gpw = 7 * sum(g) / sum(span)) %>% pull(gpw)

tax_tab <- bind_rows(
  ep %>% count(Level = "Body region (IOC)", Value = INJURY_REGION),
  ep %>% count(Level = "Tissue type (IOC)", Value = INJURY_TISSUE),
  ep %>% count(Level = "Mechanism (IOC)",   Value = INJURY_MECHANISM_IOC),
  ep %>% count(Level = "Side",              Value = INJURY_SIDE)) %>%
  group_by(Level) %>% slice_max(n, n = 6) %>%
  mutate(`%` = round(100 * n / sum(n))) %>% ungroup()
show_tbl(tax_tab, "Injury classification levels (top categories per axis, episode starts)")

# Severity, in the IOC's time-loss bands. 
sev_tab <- readRDS(file.path(BASE, "panel_2021-26.rds")) %>%
  filter(INJURY_TIMELOSS == 1, !is.na(INJURY_EPISODE_ID)) %>%
  count(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, INJURY_EPISODE_ID, name = "games_missed") %>%
  mutate(Severity = factor(injury_severity_ioc(games_missed),
                           levels = c("minimal (1-7 days)", "moderate (8-28 days)",
                                      "severe (>28 days)"))) %>%
  count(Severity) %>% mutate(`%` = round(100 * n / sum(n)))
show_tbl(sev_tab, "Severity of injury episodes, IOC time-loss bands")
```

Severity is reported, not modelled. I record it because the IOC asks for
it and because it describes the cohort honestly, but my outcome is the
onset of an injury, so severity is a property of what follows the event
rather than a predictor of it. Modelling severity would be a different
study with a different risk set.

Area of opportunity for building into the future building a dynamic
aggregation window based on injury severity.

## Defining a subsequent injury

The second half of the outcome definition is deciding when a later
absence is a new injury and when it is the old one flaring up. IOC,
distinguishes an exacerbation (same site, before recovery) from a
recurrence (same site, after the athlete has returned to full
availability).

"Full availability" is a clinical judgement: being off the injury report
does not mean the medical staff consider a player recovered, and I
observe nothing about training, rehabilitation or minutes restrictions.
So rather than assert a recovery status I do not have, I use the two
things I can observe.

First, the classification of each subsequent injury relative to the one
before it, using the data-driven level of the SIC-2.0 model (Toohey et
al. 2018, extending Finch and Cook 2014). SIC-2.0 exists precisely for
datasets without clinical input: its data-driven categories are defined
on site, nature and side alone, and the "related / unrelated" judgements
sit in a separate clinical tier which I leave unpopulated.

Second, a return-durability rule in place of a recovery judgement. What
I am counting is new episodes, and a genuine re-injury is a new episode
provided the player got back to playing properly first. So this rule
does not merge every repeat. It merges only the ones that arrive before
a player has re-established himself, which are the ones most likely to
be the original problem never having resolved. A repeat at the same site
(region and side) counts as the earlier episode flaring up if the player
managed fewer than `r RETURN_DURABILITY_GAMES` games in between;
anything after that is counted as a new episode in its own right. That
is also how the epidemiology consensus treats recurrence: Fuller et al.
(2006) classify a same-site injury after return to play as a recurrent
injury, not as a continuation.

```{r sic-table}
sic_tab <- cox %>% filter(!is.na(SIC_CATEGORY)) %>%
  count(`SIC-2.0 category` = SIC_CATEGORY, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(`%` = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
show_tbl(sic_tab, "Subsequent injuries by SIC-2.0 data-driven category")
```

Roughly one episode in five is a repeat at the same site with the same
tissue type, the category closest to a classical recurrence, and that is
before any clinical judgement about relatedness. It is the clearest
single number I have for why the recurrent-events models in Stage 4 are
worth fitting at all.

## What the risk set actually looks like

LeBron James in 2025-26 happens to contain every case: a season-opening
absence, a mid-season rest day, a region change mid-absence, and five
onsets. Read off `panel_2021-26.rds`, before the file-5 filter, so the
removed rows are still visible.

```{r risk-set-schematic, fig.height=4.6, fig.width=10}
lb <- readRDS(file.path(BASE, "panel_2021-26.rds")) %>%
  filter(PLAYER_NAME == "LeBron James", SEASON == "2025-26") %>%
  arrange(GAME_DATE) %>%
  mutate(
    g      = row_number(),
    tl     = coalesce(INJURY_TIMELOSS, 0L),
    tl_lag = dplyr::lag(tl, default = 0L),
    onset  = as.integer(coalesce(IS_NEW_INJURY, 0L) == 1 | coalesce(IS_REAGGRAVATION, 0L) == 1),
    pre1st = as.integer(cumsum(coalesce(PLAYED_FLAG, 0L)) == 0),   # left truncation
    # The file-5 rule: out only if already absent when the interval opened AND still absent.
    in_risk = as.integer(!(tl == 1 & tl_lag == 1) & pre1st == 0),
    state = case_when(
      pre1st == 1               ~ "Before first appearance (left-truncated)",
      onset == 1 & in_risk == 1 ~ "Injury onset: event, retained in risk set",
      tl == 1 & in_risk == 0    ~ "Injury absence (removed from risk set)",
      PLAYED_FLAG == 0          ~ "Non-injury absence (at risk, covariates carried forward)",
      tl_lag == 1               ~ "First game back (at risk)",
      TRUE                      ~ "Played (at risk, covariates observed)"))

lev <- c("Played (at risk, covariates observed)",
         "First game back (at risk)",
         "Non-injury absence (at risk, covariates carried forward)",
         "Injury onset: event, retained in risk set",
         "Injury absence (removed from risk set)",
         "Before first appearance (left-truncated)")
pal <- setNames(c("#3d6d99","#7fa8cc","#a8c5dd","#b2182b","#bdbdbd","#efefef"), lev)
lb$state <- factor(lb$state, levels = lev)

TILE <- 0; RISK <- -0.95
ann  <- function(x, y, lab, col = "grey15")
  annotate("text", x = x, y = y, label = lab, size = 2.8, colour = col, lineheight = 0.95)
lead <- function(x, y0, y1)
  annotate("segment", x = x, xend = x, y = y0, yend = y1, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey45")

fig_riskset <- ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = lb, aes(g, TILE, fill = state), colour = "white", linewidth = .3, height = .8) +
  geom_tile(data = lb, aes(g, RISK), height = .34, colour = "grey75", linewidth = .2,
            fill = ifelse(lb$in_risk == 1, "#2f6b3a", "white")) +
  geom_point(data = filter(lb, state == "Injury onset: event, retained in risk set"),
             aes(g, 0.62), shape = 25, size = 2.4, fill = "#b2182b", colour = "#b2182b") +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 14, y = 0.95, yend = 0.95, linewidth = .4, colour = "grey45") +
  ann(7.5, 1.62, "Season-opening\nback injury (14 games):\nevent left-truncated") +
  lead(15, 0.45, 2.30) +
  ann(15, 2.55, "Returns at game 15 and\nre-enters the risk set") +
  lead(53, 0.45, 1.05) +
  ann(53, 1.35, "Rested, not injured:\nstays in the risk set") +
  lead(64.5, 0.45, 2.30) +
  ann(64.5, 2.55, "Region changes mid-absence:\nthis onset is lost", "#a0410f") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, seq(10, 80, 10), 82), expand = expansion(add = c(3.5, 1))) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(TILE, RISK), labels = c("Scheduled\ngame", "In risk\nset"),
                     limits = c(-1.35, 3.05), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled team game within the season", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10.5) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 8.6, colour = "grey25", lineheight = .95),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.size = unit(9, "pt"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 8), legend.margin = margin(t = -2))

fig_riskset
```

Eighty-two scheduled games become `r sum(lb$in_risk)` modelled intervals
and `r sum(lb$state == "Injury onset: event, retained in risk set")`
retained events out of the seven onsets in the season. Three things are
worth reading off it.

The rest day at game 53 stays in the risk set. A rested player can still
be injured tomorrow, so dropping them would delete exactly the low-load
intervals that identify a workload effect.

Two onsets are still lost and both are design costs rather than defects.
The season-opening injury precedes any appearance, so it is
left-truncated. The game-65 onset fires mid-absence with a different
injury, so the filter takes it with the absence around it. File 5 counts
that loss on every run.

# Stage 1 - Covariate screening {#stage1}

Feeds article 2.4 and Appendix A.4.

Near-duplicate covariates destabilise a Cox model: effects split between
them, standard errors inflate, signs flip. I have several rolling
windows of the same quantity, so I screen before fitting rather than
rationalising afterwards.

I use Spearman rather than Pearson because these workload distributions
are skewed (not linear) and I care about monotone redundancy, not linear
redundancy.

```{r stage0-screening}
candidates <- c(
  "ACWR_MIN", "ROLLING_MIN_7D", "ROLLING_MIN_28D", "ROLLING_MIN_42D",
  "SEASON_CUMULATIVE_MIN", "ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "ROLLING_GAMES_28D",
  "ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "ACWR_LOAD",
  "ROLLING_INTENSITY_7D", "ROLLING_INTENSITY_28D", "INTENSITY",
  "ROLLING_DIST_7D", "ROLLING_DIST_28D", "SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
  "TEAM_DAYS_REST", "ROLLING_B2B_7D", "ROLLING_B2B_28D",
  "PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "MIN", "DISTANCE",
  "SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE", "CAREER_GAMES_MISSED", "SEASON_GAMES_MISSED",
  "PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "PLAYER_AGE_AT_GAME", "HEIGHT_INCHES", "WEIGHT",
  "PCT_THROUGH_SEASON"
)
candidates <- candidates[candidates %in% names(cox)]

cor_mat <- cor(cox[candidates], use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")
high    <- which(abs(cor_mat) > 0.8 & upper.tri(cor_mat), arr.ind = TRUE)

collinear <- tibble(
  Variable_1 = rownames(cor_mat)[high[, 1]],
  Variable_2 = colnames(cor_mat)[high[, 2]],
  Spearman_r = round(cor_mat[high], 3)
) %>% arrange(desc(abs(Spearman_r)))

show_tbl(collinear, "Collinear pairs (|Spearman r| > 0.8) - only one of each enters the model")
```

## What it shows

The pairs that breach the 0.8 threshold, cluster into a few obvious
families: the overlapping minutes windows, the career-length variables,
and the in-game effort measures. For each I keep one on interpretability
grounds rather than statistical ones:

-   `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE` with a quadratic term over age and draft year.
    Tenure carries the institutional differences in how players are
    worked, and those are not linear. The Player Participation Policy
    (2023) lets teams pre-approve back-to-back rest for older or
           high-mileage star players, so veterans are rested more by
           rule while carrying the most accumulated mileage. Two forces
           in opposite directions, which is a quadratic, not a line.
           Drakos (2010), Morikawa
    (2024) and Martin (2021) all point away from monotonicity.
-   `ROLLING_MIN_28D` over the 42-day window: 28 days is the ACWR
    convention, so results stay comparable.
-   `MIN` for in-game effort.

`ROLLING_GAMES_28D` dropped (r =
`r round(cor_mat["ROLLING_GAMES_28D", "ROLLING_MIN_28D"], 2)` with
chronic minutes), `ROLLING_GAMES_7D` kept (correlation under 0.8, and it
separates frequency from volume, since four games in a week is a
different from the same minutes across two).

-   **Neither ACWR term survives to the model.** `ACWR_LOAD` and
    `ACWR_MIN` are screened here because the acute:chronic ratio is the
    field's most cited workload construct and leaving it untested would
    be a gap. The correlation table already shows the two versions of it
    are the same variable (r =
    `r round(cor_mat["ACWR_MIN", "ACWR_LOAD"], 3)`), but the reason
    neither enters is not collinearity with each other - it is that ACWR
    is a deterministic function of the acute and chronic terms the model
    carries separately. I set out that argument where the specification
    is fixed, in Stage 2.

# Stage 2 - Nested models {#stage2}

Feeds article 2.5, 3.1, 3.2, 3.8 and Appendix B.2.

I add covariates in three domain blocks, workload, then schedule
congestion, then player context, and ask at each, whether the new domain
earns its place. Answering "which domain matters", rather than producing
one flat model where I'd be picking through 24 individually significant
coefficients.

Three specification choices carry the design, and each is a deliberate
answer to a feature of this data:

| Choice | Why it is there |
|----|----|
| `Surv(t_start, t_stop, event)` | Counting-process form, so covariates can change every game. injured this season y/n model would collapse the season to one outcome and be blind to when risk moves. |
| `strata(SEASON)` | Each season gets its own baseline hazard. The COVID-adjacent seasons had a genuinely different shape, and I don't want that contaminating the covariate effects. I assume workload acts the same way each season, not that each season is equally dangerous. |
| `cluster(PLAYER_ID)` | LeBron contributes \~332 rows that are one repeatedly-observed person, not 332 independent facts. Without this the standard errors are far too narrow. |

I also z-score every continuous covariate, so each hazard ratio reads as
"per 1 standard deviation increase". That is what makes it legitimate to
say chronic load matters more than travel, otherwise I'd be comparing an
effect measured in minutes against one measured in kilometres.

```{r zscore}
z <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(x))

cox <- cox %>%
  mutate(
    # Workload - minutes & intensity -based
    z_ROLLING_MIN_7D   = z(ROLLING_MIN_7D),
    z_ROLLING_MIN_28D  = z(ROLLING_MIN_28D),
    z_ACWR_MIN         = z(ACWR_MIN),
    z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D = z(ROLLING_GAMES_7D),
    z_MIN              = z(MIN),
    z_PREV_GAME_MIN    = z(PREV_GAME_MIN),   
    z_PREV_2GAME_MIN   = z(PREV_2GAME_MIN), 
    z_PREV_GAME_INTENSITY    = z(PREV_GAME_INTENSITY),
    z_PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY   = z(PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY),
    z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D  = z(ROLLING_LOAD_7D),
    z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D = z(ROLLING_LOAD_28D),
    z_ACWR_LOAD        = z(ACWR_LOAD),
    z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE   = z(PREV_GAME_DISTANCE),
    z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE  = z(PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE),
    # Travel
    z_ROLLING_DIST_7D        = z(ROLLING_DIST_7D),
    z_ROLLING_DIST_28D       = z(ROLLING_DIST_28D),
    z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST = z(SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST),
    # Schedule congestion
    z_IS_B2B = z(IS_B2B),
    z_ROLLING_B2B_7D               = z(ROLLING_B2B_7D),
    z_ROLLING_B2B_28D              = z(ROLLING_B2B_28D),
    z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER = z(PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER),
    z_TEAM_DAYS_REST               = z(TEAM_DAYS_REST),
    # Player context
    z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE     = z(SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE),
    z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED   = z(CAREER_GAMES_MISSED),
    z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON = z(PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON),
    z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON    = z(PCT_THROUGH_SEASON),
    z_HEIGHT_INCHES         = z(HEIGHT_INCHES),
    z_WEIGHT                = z(WEIGHT)
  )

# Two collinearity figures the prose quotes, computed here so they cannot go stale.
r_load_min <- cor(cox$ROLLING_LOAD_28D, cox$ROLLING_MIN_28D, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
r_int_load <- max(abs(cor(
  cox[c("PREV_GAME_INTENSITY", "PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY")],
  cox[c("ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "PREV_GAME_DISTANCE", "PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE")],
  use = "pairwise.complete.obs")))
```

```{r model-specs, dependson="zscore"}
surv_lhs <- "Surv(t_start, t_stop, event)"
rhs_tail <- "strata(SEASON) + cluster(PLAYER_ID)"

fit_cox <- function(covariate_terms, lhs = surv_lhs) {
  f <- as.formula(paste0(lhs, " ~ ", paste(covariate_terms, collapse = " + "),
                         " + ", rhs_tail))
  coxph(f, data = cox, ties = "efron")
}

m1_terms <- c(
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",         # acute on-court load (distance)
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",        # chronic on-court load (distance)
  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D",        # acute games played (frequency)
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D",         # acute travel load
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",        # chronic travel load
  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",  # season-long accumulated travel
  "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE",      # in-game load, last played game (lag-1, load-management signal)
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE"      # in-game load, 2 games back (lag-2, prospective fatigue spike)
)

intensity_terms <- c("z_PREV_GAME_INTENSITY", "z_PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY")

schedule_added <- c(
  "z_IS_B2B","z_ROLLING_B2B_7D", "z_ROLLING_B2B_28D",
  "z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST", "IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP"
)

context_added <- c(
  "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE", "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)",   # tenure, non-linear: Participation
                                                       # Policy rest allowances vs mileage
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",                             # career durability
  "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "RECENT_RETURN",          # prior-injury history
  "z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON", "IS_POST_ALLSTAR",           # season timing
  "PLAYED_PRESEASON", "z_HEIGHT_INCHES", "z_WEIGHT"
)

m2_terms <- c(m1_terms, schedule_added)
m3_terms <- c(m2_terms, context_added)

m3_terms_min <- c("z_ROLLING_MIN_7D", "z_ROLLING_MIN_28D",
                  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D", "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",
                  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST", "z_PREV_GAME_MIN", "z_PREV_2GAME_MIN",
                  schedule_added, context_added)
```

### What the acute and chronic load terms actually mean together

This is worth being precise about, because the two windows overlap and
that changes how the acute coefficient should be read. The 7-day window
sits inside the 28-day window: last week's load is also part of last
month's load. So the acute coefficient is not "the effect of playing a
lot last week". Holding the 28-day total fixed, it is the effect of the
same month's work being concentrated into the last week rather than
spread evenly across the four.

A worked example. Two players arrive at tonight's game having each
covered 40 km over the past month, so their chronic load is identical
and the model holds it equal:

-   Player A covered 10 km in each of the four weeks. Steady.
-   Player B covered 4 km in each of the first three weeks and 28 km
    last week. Same month, front-loaded.

They are indistinguishable on chronic load. They differ only on acute
load, and the acute coefficient is exactly the comparison of B against
A: same total work, but crammed into the days immediately before
tonight. That is what fatigue means physiologically, so this contrast is
the fatigue construct rather than a volume measure.

It also explains why the chronic term has to stay in. Fitted on its own,
acute load simply proxies for how much a player plays, and it then
predicts contact injuries just as happily as overuse ones, because busy
players collect more of everything. Conditioning on chronic strips the
volume out and leaves the concentration, which is the part fatigue can
speak to. I show that directly in the appendix.

I do not include an acute:chronic workload ratio. ACWR is by
construction a function of the two terms already in the model (weekly
acute over weekly-average chronic), so adding it puts the same
information in three times, and it distorts the chronic coefficient
rather than adding anything. The concentration-versus-volume contrast
above captures what the ratio was meant to capture, without the
redundancy.

In-game load is lagged, not contemporaneous. The current game's distance
is reverse-caused (a player who breaks down logs a low distance in the
game it happens) so it reads protective for the wrong reason. I use the
last played game and two played games back. Both are known before the
interval opens, and they separate two signals: lag-1 carries the
load-management pattern, so should read protective through selection;
lag-2 sits before that compromise, where a real fatigue spike should
show. Cost: first two games each season drop out.

Intensity (distance per minute) is deliberately out of the primary
model, and tested separately below. It is close to orthogonal to load
(\|r\| ≤ `r round(r_int_load, 2)`) so it is a real construct, not a
relabel, but a per-game rate needs a base of minutes to mean anything (I
require 10+, which makes it more missing than the load terms) and the
rolling windows were null.

The schedule block carries both the accumulated dose and the
point-in-time flags, deliberately. The dose is the exposure measure. The
flags are contaminated by coaching decisions, since a coach rests an
at-risk player tonight. I keep them so the contrast is visible in the
results rather than hidden by dropping them, and mark them
selection-biased wherever they appear.

## Model 1 - Workload

```{r m1, dependson="model-specs"}
m1 <- fit_cox(m1_terms)
summary(m1)
```

## Model 2 - Workload + Schedule

```{r m2, dependson="model-specs"}
m2 <- fit_cox(m2_terms)
summary(m2)
```

## Model 3 - Workload + Schedule + Player context

```{r m3, dependson="model-specs"}
m3 <- fit_cox(m3_terms)
summary(m3)
```

## Does each domain earn its place?

A likelihood-ratio test is not valid here. `cluster(PLAYER_ID)` does not
change the likelihood, only the variance estimated afterwards, so an LRT
would read the uncorrected likelihood diregarding the clustering
adjustment. I use a robust Wald test on the newly-added block instead,
built from the clustered covariance, plus the change in concordance.

```{r nested-tests, dependson=c("m1","m2","m3")}
# Joint H0 test that the coefficients in a model are all zero, using the robust (clustered) covariance. 
robust_wald <- function(model, added_terms) {
  cf   <- coef(model)
  norm <- function(s) gsub("\\s", "", s)      # I(x^2) spacing varies; match robustly
  idx  <- which(norm(names(cf)) %in% norm(added_terms))
  V    <- vcov(model)[idx, idx, drop = FALSE] # robust vcov of just those coefficients
  b    <- cf[idx]
  stat <- as.numeric(t(b) %*% solve(V) %*% b) # Wald statistic: b' V^-1 b
  tibble(block_df = length(idx), wald_chisq = round(stat, 2),
         p_value  = signif(pchisq(stat, length(idx), lower.tail = FALSE), 4))
}

nested <- bind_rows(
  robust_wald(m2, schedule_added) %>% mutate(block = "Schedule (added to Model 1)"),
  robust_wald(m3, context_added)  %>% mutate(block = "Player context (added to Model 2)")
) %>%
  select(block, block_df, wald_chisq, p_value) %>%
  mutate(p_value = fmt_p(p_value))

concordance_progression <- tibble(
  Model = c("Model 1 - workload", "Model 2 - + schedule", "Model 3 - + player context"),
  Concordance = c(summary(m1)$concordance[1],
                  summary(m2)$concordance[1],
                  summary(m3)$concordance[1]) %>% round(4)
)

show_tbl(nested, "Robust Wald tests on each added block")
show_tbl(concordance_progression, "Discrimination as each domain is added")
```

```{r m3-hr, dependson="m3"}
m3_tidy <- tidy(m3, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(effect_size = abs(estimate - 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(effect_size)) %>%
  select(term, HR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value, robust.se) %>%
  mutate(p.value = fmt_p(p.value))

show_tbl(m3_tidy, "Model 3 - hazard ratios, sorted by effect size (not by p)")
```

## What it shows

Both blocks earn their place and concordance climbs to
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 3)`: given two comparable
intervals, the model ranks the one that gets injured higher about
`r round(100 * summary(m3)$concordance[1])`% of the time against 50% by
chance. From public box-score and schedule data alone, no GPS, no
medical screening, no training load, I read that as close to the honest
ceiling. Establishing where that ceiling sits is itself worth knowing.

Chronic 28-day load is the headline at HR
`r round(summary(m3)$conf.int["z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", 1], 1)` per SD.

Two point-in-time flags read protective, the back-to-back and the
road-trip flag. Playing the second night of a back-to-back is not safer.
It is health-gating, since a coach sits a player carrying something, so
the flag partly records who was judged fit. Both vary between team-mates
on the same date, which is the tell. This is why I interpret the
accumulated dose measures instead.

Team days rest is the opposite case. Protective at HR
`r hr(m3, "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST")`, which is what physiology predicts rather
than a puzzle, and it is the one schedule covariate that cannot be
health-gated: it comes off the fixture list and every team-mate shares
it on a given date. Its SD is about a day, so that is roughly 13% lower
hazard per extra rest day, against Lewis (2018) reporting 15.96% lower
odds on different seasons with a different model. On the one covariate
where selection is ruled out by construction, an independent estimate
comes back almost exactly. No asterisk.

`RECENT_RETURN` is the clearest case of the same thing. A player in the
fortnight after returning carries HR `r hr(m3, "RECENT_RETURN")`, lower
hazard, against a literature expecting return-to-play to be high risk.
Nobody returns before medical staff clear them and nobody comes back to
a full load. It measures who was permitted to play, not whether
returning is safe, and carries the same selection asterisk.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 3 - The proportional-hazards assumption {#stage3}

Feeds article 2.6, 3.3 and Appendix B.1.

Cox assumes each covariate's effect is constant over time: heavy chronic
load as dangerous in game 70 as in game 10. Testable with scaled
Schoenfeld residuals, which ask whether the covariate values of the
players who fail drift as the season progresses.

A violation here would be a finding, not a problem, since it would mean
a risk factor intensifies or fades across a season, which only the
time-to-event framing can surface. I went in hoping to find one.

`transform = "identity"` keeps the axis as raw game number, so the
plotted trend is readable against any time-interaction I might fit.

```{r ph-tests, dependson=c("m1","m2","m3")}
zph1 <- cox.zph(m1, transform = "identity")
zph2 <- cox.zph(m2, transform = "identity")
zph3 <- cox.zph(m3, transform = "identity")

zph3_tab <- as.data.frame(zph3$table) %>%
  rownames_to_column("term") %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(flag = if_else(term != "GLOBAL" & p < 0.05, "** VIOLATES", "")) %>%
  arrange(term == "GLOBAL", p)

plot_terms <- zph3_tab %>% filter(term != "GLOBAL") %>% pull(term)  # GLOBAL has no curve to plot

zph3_tab %>%
  mutate(chisq = round(chisq, 2), p = fmt_p(p)) %>%
  show_tbl("Model 3 - proportional-hazards test (scaled Schoenfeld residuals)")
```

`r sum(zph3_tab$flag != "")` individual covariates flagged at p \< 0.05
(the two lag in-game load terms among them, at p =
`r fmt_p(zph3_tab$p[zph3_tab$term == "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE"])` and
`r fmt_p(zph3_tab$p[zph3_tab$term == "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE"])`).

## The plots, which is where the decision actually got made

A p-value only says the slope is not exactly zero, and at
`r format(m3$nevent, big.mark = ",")` events a near-flat line still
tests significant. Shape is what matters, so I plot every term: flat
means the assumption holds, sloping means the effect drifts.

```{r schoenfeld-plots, dependson="ph-tests", fig.height=4.2, fig.width=7.5, results="hold"}
for (v in plot_terms) {
  idx <- which(rownames(zph3$table) == v)
  plot(zph3[idx], resid = FALSE, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
       main = paste0("Schoenfeld: ", v, "  (effect vs game number)"))
  abline(h = 0, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
}
```

## What it shows, and why I remedied nothing

The global test was always going to reject at
`r format(m3$nevent, big.mark = ",")` events (p =
`r fmt_p(zph3_tab$p[zph3_tab$term == "GLOBAL"])`), and
`r sum(zph3_tab$flag != "")` terms flag individually. Significance is
not the question here. What settles it is the shape of each drift and
whether any of it is biological. Decomposing by drift direction says it
is not.

```{r ph-decomp, dependson=c("ph-tests","m3")}
# Direction of each violation: does beta(t) weaken TOWARD zero (the effect fading) 
bhat <- coef(m3)
vt   <- zph3_tab %>% filter(flag != "") %>% pull(term)
slope_sign <- sapply(vt, function(v) sign(cov(zph3$x, zph3$y[, match(v, colnames(zph3$y))])))
reading <- tribble(
  ~term,                            ~Reading,
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",          "Durability history - frailty compression",
  "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE",           "Load-management signal - selection",
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",          "Fatigue-spike signal - selection",
  "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE",            "Experience - survivor pool",
  "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)",       "Experience curvature",
  "z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "Availability marker",
  "IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP",            "Availability marker - sharpening",
  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D",             "~zero effect (direction immaterial)",
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D",              "~zero effect (direction immaterial)",
  "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON",        "Prior-injury history - frailty compression",
  "IS_POST_ALLSTAR",                "Season phase - context, not a risk factor",
  "z_IS_B2B",                       "Availability marker - selection",
  "PLAYED_PRESEASON",               "Pre-season availability - selection",
  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",       "Accumulated travel - exposure",
  "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST",               "Availability marker - selection",
  "RECENT_RETURN",                  "Prior-injury history - frailty compression",
  "z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON",           "Season phase - context, not a risk factor",
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",              "Acute load",
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",             "Chronic load",
  "z_ROLLING_B2B_7D",               "Congestion dose - exposure",
  "z_ROLLING_B2B_28D",              "Congestion dose - exposure",
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",             "Chronic travel - exposure",
  "z_HEIGHT_INCHES",                "Anthropometry",
  "z_WEIGHT",                       "Anthropometry")
decomp <- tibble(term = vt, `HR (per SD)` = round(exp(bhat[vt]), 2),
                 Drift = ifelse(slope_sign != sign(bhat[vt]), "toward 0", "away")) %>%
  left_join(reading, by = "term") %>%
  mutate(Term = sub("z_", "", term),
         Reading = coalesce(Reading, "(unclassified)")) %>%   # never print a bare NA
  select(Term, `HR (per SD)`, Drift, Reading)
n_toward <- sum(decomp$Drift == "toward 0"); n_viol <- nrow(decomp)
show_tbl(decomp, "PH violators by drift direction - all selection or context, none biological")

# Let acute load's effect differ early vs late in the season.
cut <- median(cox$t_stop)
cox$.period <- factor(ifelse(cox$t_stop <= cut, "early", "late"), levels = c("early", "late"))
f_plain <- as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "), " + ", rhs_tail))
ss_e <- exp(coef(coxph(f_plain, data = filter(cox, .period == "early"), ties = "efron"))["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"])
ss_l <- exp(coef(coxph(f_plain, data = filter(cox, .period == "late"),  ties = "efron"))["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"])
m_iso <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ",
          paste(c(setdiff(m3_terms, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D*.period"), collapse = " + "),
          " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox, ties = "efron")
iso_e <- exp(coef(m_iso)["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"])
iso_l <- exp(coef(m_iso)["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"] + coef(m_iso)[grep(":\\.period", names(coef(m_iso)))])
cidx <- function(fit, d) { d$.lp <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = d, type = "lp"))
  concordance(Surv(t_start, t_stop, event) ~ .lp, data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance }
tr <- filter(cox, SEASON != "2025-26"); te <- filter(cox, SEASON == "2025-26")
oos_b <- cidx(coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
          " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")), data = tr, ties = "efron"), te)
oos_s <- cidx(coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ",
          paste(c(setdiff(m3_terms, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D*.period"), collapse = " + "),
          " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")), data = tr, ties = "efron"), te)
```

Three points close the case for reporting the proportional model:

1.  The drift is selection. `r n_toward` of the `r n_viol` violators
    weaken toward zero, which is survivor and frailty compression: as
    the most injury-prone players leave the pool, the durability and
    history effects fade. Those sharpening away are availability
    markers, and two sit on covariates with no effect at all (HR ≈ 1.0,
    where direction is meaningless).

2.  The covariates carrying the causal claim are stable. Chronic load p
    = `r fmt_p(zph3_tab$p[zph3_tab$term == "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"])`,
    acute load p =
    `r fmt_p(zph3_tab$p[zph3_tab$term == "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"])`. Every
    violation sits on a term I already decline to read causally.

3.  The standard remedy buys nothing, and I fitted it to find out. The
    usual fix for a violation is to let the coefficient change with
    time. I tested it on acute load, splitting the season in half.

    Two ways, and the gap between them is the instructive part. Refit
    the whole model on each half and the drift looks real: HR
    `r round(ss_e, 2)` early against `r round(ss_l, 2)` late. But that
    lets every coefficient move, so acute load is soaking up movement
    from everywhere else. Fit one model and let only acute load interact
    with season half and it nearly vanishes: `r round(iso_e, 2)` against
    `r round(iso_l, 2)`. Most of the drift was never acute load's.

    The held-out season settles it: concordance `r round(oos_b, 4)`
    proportional against `r round(oos_s, 4)` with the time-varying term.
    Nothing changes. A time-varying coefficient here would fit the
    selection rather than remove it.

The season dynamic is real but lives in the baseline hazard (quantified
in Stage 6), which `strata(SEASON)` already absorbs. A bad chronic load
is a bad chronic load whenever in the season it lands.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 4 - Reporting and calibration {#stage4}

Feeds article 3.4 and Appendix B.5.

No classic absolute-risk calibration curve, which is a design
consequence: `strata(SEASON)` gives five baseline hazards, and each row
is a game-interval rather than a person, so "predicted 30-day risk" is
not well defined. What the design supports is relative-hazard
calibration: group intervals by risk score, check the observed event
rate climbs across groups.

```{r calibration, dependson="m3"}
cstat <- summary(m3)$concordance
c_est <- cstat[1]; c_se <- cstat[2]
c_lo  <- c_est - 1.96 * c_se; c_hi <- c_est + 1.96 * c_se

# knitr caches the fitted model but not the environment its formula points at, so a
# cached m3 cannot rebuild its model frame and predict() fails with "object 'cox' not
# found". Re-point the terms environment at this chunk, where cox is loaded.
attr(m3$terms, ".Environment") <- environment()

cox_lp <- cox %>%
  mutate(risk_score = as.numeric(predict(m3, newdata = ., type = "lp"))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(risk_score))

calib <- cox_lp %>%
  mutate(risk_group = ntile(risk_score, 10)) %>%
  group_by(risk_group) %>%
  summarise(
    n_intervals     = n(),
    events          = sum(event),
    event_rate_1k   = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 2),
    mean_risk_score = round(mean(risk_score), 3),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

mono <- cor(calib$risk_group, calib$event_rate_1k, method = "spearman")
show_tbl(calib, "Relative-hazard calibration: observed event rate by risk-score decile")
```

```{r calibration-plot, dependson="calibration", fig.height=4.5, fig.width=7}
fig_calib <- ggplot(calib, aes(risk_group, event_rate_1k)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  labs(title = "Observed injury rate rises monotonically with predicted risk",
       subtitle = paste0("Spearman correlation with decile rank = ", round(mono, 3)),
       x = "Risk-score decile (1 = lowest predicted risk)",
       y = "Observed events per 1,000 intervals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

fig_calib
```

```{r hr-table, dependson="m3"}
domain_map <- tribble(
  ~term,                            ~domain,          ~label,
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",              "Workload",       "Acute on-court load (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",             "Workload",       "Chronic on-court load (28d)",
  "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D",             "Workload",       "Acute games played (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D",              "Workload",       "Acute travel load (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_DIST_28D",             "Workload",       "Chronic travel load (28d)",
  "z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",       "Workload",       "Season cumulative travel",
  "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE",           "Workload",       "In-game load, last game *",
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",          "Workload",       "In-game load, 2 games back",
  "z_ROLLING_B2B_7D",               "Schedule",       "Acute back-to-back dose (7d)",
  "z_ROLLING_B2B_28D",              "Schedule",       "Chronic back-to-back dose (28d)",
  "z_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER", "Schedule",       "Road-trip game number",
  "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST",               "Schedule",       "Team days rest",
  "z_IS_B2B",                       "Schedule",       "Back-to-back (point-in-time) *",
  "IS_PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP",            "Schedule",       "On road trip (point-in-time) *",
  "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE",            "Player context", "Experience (seasons)",
  "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)",       "Player context", "Experience squared (inverted-U)",
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",          "Player context", "Career games missed (durability)",
  "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON",        "Player context", "Prior injury episodes this season",
  "RECENT_RETURN",                  "Player context", "Recently returned (<=14d) *",
  "z_PCT_THROUGH_SEASON",           "Player context", "Season progress",
  "IS_POST_ALLSTAR",                "Player context", "Post-All-Star phase",
  "PLAYED_PRESEASON",               "Player context", "Played pre-season",
  "z_HEIGHT_INCHES",                "Player context", "Height",
  "z_WEIGHT",                       "Player context", "Weight"
)

hr_tab <- tidy(m3, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  select(term, HR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) %>%
  left_join(domain_map, by = "term") %>%
  mutate(domain  = factor(domain, levels = c("Workload", "Schedule", "Player context")),
         across(c(HR, conf.low, conf.high), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  arrange(domain, desc(abs(log(HR)))) %>%
  mutate(p.value = fmt_p(p.value)) %>%
  select(domain, label, HR, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

show_tbl(hr_tab, "Final hazard ratios (Model 3), by domain - * = selection-biased")

write.csv(hr_tab, file.path(BASE, "final_hazard_ratios_model3.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

## What it shows

Concordance is `r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4)` (95% CI
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1] - 1.96 * summary(m3)$concordance[2], 3)`-`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1] + 1.96 * summary(m3)$concordance[2], 3)`),
and the risk score orders observed hazard almost perfectly across
deciles (Spearman 1). The model reliably sorts high-risk from low-risk
intervals even though it cannot state an absolute probability. For an
operational use case, who should be managed this week, ranking is the
suitable.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 5 - Recurrent events and frailty {#stage5}

Feeds article 2.6, 3.6 and Appendix B.4.

Model 3 counts only first new injuries, which throws information away:
players get hurt repeatedly and that repetition is what the applied
literature cares about most. Rather than pick one recurrent-events model
and hope, I fit three that assume different things.

-   Andersen-Gill - every onset counts, common baseline, marginal. "What
    raises the hazard of any injury onset?"
-   PWP gap-time - baseline stratified by event order, clock reset after
    each event. "Is a second injury different from a first?"
-   Shared frailty - per-player random intercept. Its variance θ is a
    single-number measure of unobserved proneness, which is the Martin
    (2021) claim made testable.

```{r ag-model, dependson="model-specs"}
m3_ag <- fit_cox(m3_terms, lhs = "Surv(t_start, t_stop, event_recurrent)")

ag_compare <- full_join(
  tidy(m3,    exponentiate = TRUE) %>% select(term, HR_new_injury = estimate),
  tidy(m3_ag, exponentiate = TRUE) %>% select(term, HR_all_injury = estimate),
  by = "term"
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

show_tbl(ag_compare, "Primary (new injury) vs Andersen-Gill (all injury)")
```

```{r pwp, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
# PWP gap-time: within each player-season, ep_order counts which spell this is, and
# the clock restarts at each event so "time" becomes games since the last injury.
pwp <- cox %>%
  arrange(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, t_stop) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID) %>%
  mutate(ep_order = 1L + cumsum(dplyr::lag(event_recurrent, default = 0L))) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, ep_order) %>%
  mutate(gap_stop  = row_number(),
         gap_start = gap_stop - 1L) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(ep_order_capped = factor(pmin(ep_order, 3L), levels = 1:3,
                                  labels = c("1st", "2nd", "3rd+")))

stopifnot(all(pwp$gap_stop > pwp$gap_start), all(pwp$gap_start >= 0))

# Drop prior-episode covariates: the event-order strata and the reset clock already show "how many prior injuries" and "how long since"
pwp_terms <- setdiff(m3_terms, c("z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "RECENT_RETURN"))

pwp_fit <- coxph(
  as.formula(paste0("Surv(gap_start, gap_stop, event_recurrent) ~ ",
                    paste(pwp_terms, collapse = " + "),
                    " + strata(SEASON, ep_order_capped) + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")),
  data = pwp, ties = "efron"
)

pwp %>%
  group_by(ep_order_capped) %>%
  summarise(rows = n(), events = sum(event_recurrent),
            `Rate per 1,000` = round(1000 * events / rows, 1), .groups = "drop") %>%
  show_tbl("Events by injury-spell stratum")
```

### What the spell strata do to the baseline

`strata(SEASON, ep_order_capped)` is the part of this model I find most
informative, and it is easy to skim past because it produces no
coefficient at all. Stratifying tells the model to fit a separate
baseline hazard for a player's 1st, 2nd and 3rd-or-later spell, while
sharing the covariate effects across them. Nothing about being on your
third injury of the season is charged to a workload term; it is absorbed
into the shape of the baseline. So if the baselines separate, that is
recurrence risk showing up in a place no covariate can explain away.

They separate a lot.

```{r pwp-baseline, dependson="pwp"}
GAP_AT <- 10   # read the baselines at a common gap-time: 10 games back from injury

pwp_base <- basehaz(pwp_fit, centered = FALSE) %>% as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(Spell = case_when(grepl("1st", strata) ~ "1st",
                           grepl("2nd", strata) ~ "2nd",
                           grepl("3rd", strata) ~ "3rd+")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Spell), time <= GAP_AT) %>%
  group_by(strata, Spell) %>% summarise(H = max(hazard), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(Spell) %>% summarise(H = mean(H), .groups = "drop") %>%   # average over seasons
  mutate(`Baseline cumulative hazard` = round(H, 4),
         `Relative to 1st spell` = round(H / H[Spell == "1st"], 2)) %>%
  select(-H)
show_tbl(pwp_base, paste0("Baseline hazard by injury spell, at gap-time ", GAP_AT,
                          " games (covariate effects held equal)"))

esc2 <- pwp_base$`Relative to 1st spell`[pwp_base$Spell == "2nd"]
esc3 <- pwp_base$`Relative to 1st spell`[pwp_base$Spell == "3rd+"]

# Crude (unadjusted) rates for the same strata, so the prose can compare how much of
# the escalation the covariates actually absorb.
crude <- pwp %>% group_by(ep_order_capped) %>%
  summarise(r = round(1000 * sum(event_recurrent) / n(), 1), .groups = "drop")
crude_1st <- crude$r[crude$ep_order_capped == "1st"]
crude_3rd <- crude$r[crude$ep_order_capped == "3rd+"]
```

Ten games after returning, and holding every workload, schedule and
context covariate equal, a player in their second spell carries
`r esc2`x the baseline hazard of a player in their first, and a player
in their third or later spell carries `r esc3`x. The unadjusted picture
is steeper still. Crude event rates go from `r crude_1st` per 1,000
intervals in a first spell to `r crude_3rd` in a third, an escalation of
`r round(crude_3rd / crude_1st, 1)`x against the `r esc3`x that survives
adjustment. So the covariates do absorb a real share of it, roughly
`r round(100 * (crude_3rd/crude_1st - esc3) / (crude_3rd/crude_1st))`%:
players on their third injury of a season are carrying heavier workloads
and worse schedules, and the model can see that. What it cannot see is
the remaining `r esc3`x, which sits in the baseline where no covariate
reaches it.

That is the clearest statement this thesis can make of a finding the
injury-epidemiology literature has reported repeatedly: previous injury
is among the strongest predictors of the next one (Fulton et al. 2014;
Hägglund et al. 2006), and in the NBA specifically Eftekhari et al.
(2022) found that 81.4% of players who sustained a hamstring injury went
on to sustain a subsequent injury in the same or following season. The
practical reading is uncomfortable but simple: the single largest change
in a player's risk profile is having already been injured once, and it
is a change no amount of load management shows up as, because it is not
carried by the load covariates at all.

```{r frailty, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
#a random intercept per player.
frail_fit <- coxme(
  as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, event_recurrent) ~ ",
                    paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
                    " + strata(SEASON) + (1 | PLAYER_ID)")),
  data = cox, ties = "efron"
)

theta    <- as.numeric(unlist(frail_fit$vcoef))[1]
sd_frail <- sqrt(theta)
frail_fit
```

A θ on its own is uninterpretable: it says how much players differ in
what I could not measure, not how much of the original difference I
removed. So I refit with the blocks added one at a time from nothing,
all on the same rows, otherwise the variances are not comparable.

```{r frailty-nested, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
# Common row set, so theta is comparable across specifications.
need_f <- gsub("I\\(|\\^2\\)", "", unique(m3_terms))
d_f <- cox %>% filter(if_all(all_of(intersect(need_f, names(cox))), ~ !is.na(.)))

theta_of <- function(terms) {
  rhs <- if (length(terms))
    paste(paste(terms, collapse = " + "), "+ strata(SEASON) + (1 | PLAYER_ID)")
  else "strata(SEASON) + (1 | PLAYER_ID)"
  fit <- coxme(as.formula(paste("Surv(t_start, t_stop, event_recurrent) ~", rhs)),
               data = d_f, ties = "efron")
  as.numeric(unlist(fit$vcoef))[1]
}

theta_steps <- c(`No covariates (baseline)` = theta_of(character(0)),
                 `+ Workload`               = theta_of(m1_terms),
                 `+ Schedule congestion`    = theta_of(m2_terms),
                 `+ Player context (full)`  = theta_of(m3_terms))

frailty_tab <- tibble(
  Model = names(theta_steps),
  theta = round(theta_steps, 3),
  `SD (log hazard)` = round(sqrt(theta_steps), 3),
  `Hazard, +1 SD of proneness` = round(exp(sqrt(theta_steps)), 2),
  `90th vs 10th percentile` = round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps)), 2)
)
pct_absorbed <- round(100 * (theta_steps[1] - theta_steps[4]) / theta_steps[1])
show_tbl(frailty_tab, paste0("Between-player heterogeneity as covariates are added (",
                             pct_absorbed, "% of the baseline variance absorbed)"))
```

```{r recurrent-compare, dependson=c("ag-model","pwp","frailty")}
headline <- c("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D", "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",
              "z_ROLLING_GAMES_7D", "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED", "z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE",
              "z_TEAM_DAYS_REST", "z_IS_B2B", "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "RECENT_RETURN")

hr_from <- function(cf, nm) if (nm %in% names(cf)) round(exp(cf[[nm]]), 3) else NA_real_

compare <- tibble(
  term       = headline,
  HR_AG      = map_dbl(headline, ~ hr_from(coef(m3_ag),    .x)),
  HR_PWP     = map_dbl(headline, ~ hr_from(coef(pwp_fit),  .x)),
  HR_frailty = map_dbl(headline, ~ hr_from(fixef(frail_fit), .x))
)

show_tbl(compare, "Cross-model comparison - AG (marginal) vs PWP (spell strata) vs frailty (conditional)")
```

## What it shows

The headline workload effects hold their shape across all three, the
chronic-load result is not an artefact of how I chose to handle
recurrence.

The frailty variance θ = `r round(theta, 3)` is the most interesting
number in this section, but only once it is read against the baseline.
With no covariates at all, θ is `r round(theta_steps[1], 3)`, which puts
the 90th percentile of injury-proneness at
`r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps[1])), 1)`x the hazard of
the 10th. With the full covariate set that spread falls to
`r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sd_frail), 1)`x. The model absorbs
`r pct_absorbed`% of the between-player variance.

Player context does most of that work, taking θ from
`r round(theta_steps[3], 3)` to `r round(theta_steps[4], 3)`, more than
workload and schedule combined. Which is what should happen: career
games missed, tenure and prior-episode history are player-level
attributes, so they are the only terms with real purchase on
between-player differences. Workload moves around within a player across
a season.

Worth setting the residual against something measured. One SD of
unmeasured proneness multiplies hazard by `r round(exp(sd_frail), 2)`;
one SD of chronic load by `r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")`. The biggest
thing I measure is bigger than the biggest thing I miss. What is left is
a real `r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sd_frail), 1)`x spread that public
data does not reach, which is a limit rather than a failure.

`CAREER_GAMES_MISSED` is the instructive divergence:
`r compare$HR_AG[compare$term == "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED"]` under AG,
`r compare$HR_frailty[compare$term == "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED"]` under
frailty. Not a contradiction, two questions. AG is marginal (across the
population, more games missed means higher risk); frailty is conditional
(holding a player's own proneness fixed, it adds nothing). Career games
missed is largely a proxy for the frailty term, so once frailty is
estimated the proxy has no work left.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 6 - Mechanism split and hazard trajectory {#stage6}

Feeds article 2.6, 3.4 and 3.5. This is the identification strategy.

This is the stage that tests my hypothesis hardest, and where I most
expected to be wrong.

The negative control. If workload genuinely causes injury, its effect
should depend on injury type: strong for overuse injuries, weaker for
injuries that are essentially random contact events. If instead workload
predicts every injury type equally, including a finger fracture from a
loose ball, then what I am measuring is not fatigue but exposure:
high-load players are on court more, so more things happen to them.

The tiers are cut on mechanism, following the IOC consensus statement
(Bahr et al. 2020), which asks for mechanism to be recorded as acute,
repetitive, or a mix of the two, and explicitly warns against a simple
sudden/gradual dichotomy.

The repetitive tier is reported in **two columns**, and that split
turned out to matter more than anything else in this stage. Only about a
fifth of it is a pathology anyone actually named; the rest is symptom
text. A column of four, then:

1.  **Overuse, diagnosed** - a named overuse pathology: tendinopathy,
    plantar fasciopathy, bursitis, stress fracture or stress reaction.
    If accumulated workload causes injury, this is where the effect
    belongs.
2.  **Overuse, symptom only** - the same mechanism label, but the report
    records only "soreness", "tightness" or "spasms" with no diagnosis
    attached. Whether these are incident pathology or a precautionary
    rest decision written down as soreness is exactly the question, and
    keeping them separate is what lets the table answer it.
3.  **Acute non-contact** - a discrete event that fatigue can plausibly
    set up: strains, sprains, and non-contact tears. The IOC's "mixed"
    case, an acute failure of a cumulatively loaded tissue.
4.  **Acute impact** - external energy transfer: contusions,
    lacerations, concussion, and fractures or dislocations at
    contact-prone sites. Workload cannot cause a jammed finger or a
    facial laceration, so this is the negative control.

Only the overuse tier splits this way. My classifier sends all vague
symptom text to "repetitive" by construction, so acute non-contact and
acute impact are already about 95% named pathology and there is nothing
to separate; splitting them would be a distinction without a difference,
on strata far too small to fit.

A null result on the control would support a causal reading of the
workload effect. A positive result detects confounding. So the control
is doing its job either way, and the reader should judge it on whether
it can detect bias, not on whether it comes out empty.

If injuries workload cannot cause are essentially pure exposure, then
the impact column is an estimate of the exposure component itself, and
any covariate that fails to exceed it is not showing anything I am
entitled to call causal. The two ratio columns do that division.

Contact versus non-contact is not always recoverable from a public
injury report: an ankle sprain can be landing awkwardly or landing on
someone's foot, and the report says only "Left Ankle; Sprain". I assign
each episode on the balance of the recorded pathology and the site, so
the control tier is indicative rather than exact.

The trajectory. `basehaz()` reads the baseline hazard directly, telling
me when in a season risk elevates for an average player, independent of
any covariate.

```{r mechanism, dependson=c("zscore","model-specs")}
# Mechanism models use the EXACT Model 3 specification (m3_terms): one specification,
# four outcomes, so every column is directly comparable to Model 3 and to each other.
#
# The repetitive tier is split. 
named_path <- !cox$INJURY_TISSUE %in% c("non_specific", "not_recorded")
cox$ev_rep_named <- as.integer(cox$event_repetitive == 1 &  named_path)
cox$ev_rep_vague <- as.integer(cox$event_repetitive == 1 & !named_path)

fit_outcome <- function(outcome, terms) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ ",
                          paste(terms, collapse = " + "), " + ", rhs_tail)),
        data = cox, ties = "efron")
}

m_rep_named <- fit_outcome("ev_rep_named",     m3_terms)  # diagnosed overuse
m_rep_vague <- fit_outcome("ev_rep_vague",     m3_terms)  # symptom report only
m_load      <- fit_outcome("event_acute_nc",   m3_terms)  # acute non-contact
m_impact    <- fit_outcome("event_acute_imp",  m3_terms)  # acute impact = the control
m_soft      <- fit_outcome("event_repetitive", m3_terms)  # pooled, for the trajectory below

m_soft_recurrent   <- fit_outcome("event_repetitive_recurrent", m3_terms)
m_load_recurrent   <- fit_outcome("event_acute_nc_recurrent",   m3_terms)
m_impact_recurrent <- fit_outcome("event_acute_imp_recurrent",  m3_terms)

mech_terms <- tribble(
  ~term,                     ~label,
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D",      "Chronic load (28d)",
  "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D",       "Acute load (7d)",
  "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",   "In-game load, 2 games back",
  "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON", "Prior injury episodes",
  "z_CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",   "Career games missed",
  "IS_POST_ALLSTAR",         "Post-All-Star phase")

mods <- list(m_rep_named, m_rep_vague, m_load, m_impact)
nms  <- c("Overuse (diagnosed)", "Overuse (symptom only)", "Acute non-contact",
          "Acute impact (control)")

# Built as character throughout: the p-value / concordance / event rows appended below
# are text, and bind_rows will not combine a numeric column with a character one.
fmt2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)

mech_tab <- mech_terms %>%
  mutate(!!nms[1] := map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_rep_named, .x)),
         !!nms[2] := map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_rep_vague, .x)),
         !!nms[3] := map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_load,      .x)),
         !!nms[4] := map_dbl(term, ~ hr(m_impact,    .x)),
         `Diagnosed / control`   = .data[[nms[1]]] / .data[[nms[4]]],
         `Non-contact / control` = .data[[nms[3]]] / .data[[nms[4]]]) %>%
  select(` ` = label, all_of(nms), `Diagnosed / control`, `Non-contact / control`) %>%
  mutate(across(-1, fmt2))

acute_p <- map_chr(mods, ~ fmt_p(summary(.x)$coefficients["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "Pr(>|z|)"]))

mech_tab <- bind_rows(
  mech_tab,
  tibble(` ` = "Acute load p-value", !!nms[1] := acute_p[1], !!nms[2] := acute_p[2],
         !!nms[3] := acute_p[3], !!nms[4] := acute_p[4],
         `Diagnosed / control` = NA_character_, `Non-contact / control` = NA_character_),
  tibble(` ` = "Concordance (C)",
         !!nms[1] := as.character(round(summary(m_rep_named)$concordance[1], 3)),
         !!nms[2] := as.character(round(summary(m_rep_vague)$concordance[1], 3)),
         !!nms[3] := as.character(round(summary(m_load)$concordance[1], 3)),
         !!nms[4] := as.character(round(summary(m_impact)$concordance[1], 3)),
         `Diagnosed / control` = NA_character_, `Non-contact / control` = NA_character_),
  tibble(` ` = "Events",
         !!nms[1] := as.character(sum(cox$ev_rep_named)),
         !!nms[2] := as.character(sum(cox$ev_rep_vague)),
         !!nms[3] := as.character(sum(cox$event_acute_nc)),
         !!nms[4] := as.character(sum(cox$event_acute_imp)),
         `Diagnosed / control` = NA_character_, `Non-contact / control` = NA_character_))

show_tbl(mech_tab, "Mechanism split (IOC axis), benchmarked against the negative control")
```

The control fired, and that is the result. Chronic load returns
`r hr(m_impact, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` on injuries workload cannot
cause, which is larger than the
`r hr(m_rep_named, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` it returns on diagnosed
overuse, the injuries it is supposed to cause. A month of heavy load
does not fracture a finger, so that
`r hr(m_impact, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` cannot be fatigue. It is exposure
and health selection: players carrying a heavy 28-day load are the ones
on court when a loose ball or a stray elbow arrives, and they are
carrying that load precisely because they were fit enough to keep being
selected. Chronic load is therefore not something I can read causally at
all, in any tier - the control tells me the whole of it could be
exposure.

Acute load is the exception, and splitting the overuse tier is what
makes it visible. Where a pathology is actually named, acute load is the
largest in the whole analysis (`r hr(m_rep_named, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`,
p =
`r fmt_p(summary(m_rep_named)$coefficients["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "Pr(>|z|)"])`),
larger even than for acute non-contact. Where the report says only that
something is sore, it is flat (`r hr(m_rep_vague, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`,
p =
`r fmt_p(summary(m_rep_vague)$coefficients["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "Pr(>|z|)"])`).
Pooled, those two average out to something weak and ambiguous. Acute
load is both largest and significant on the two tiers where fatigue can
plausibly act, and both small and indistinguishable from zero on the
symptom-only tier and on the control. The two together are what make the
pattern read as specificity rather than noise.

The load-overuse relationship is real, but only visible when the outcome
is a diagnosed pathology rather than a symptom report. That is a finding
about measurement as much as physiology, and it is the most practically
useful thing in this section: a surveillance system built on
availability text will understate the workload effect on overuse injury,
because most of what it records as overuse is not a diagnosis. Two
things support reading the symptom-only column as something other than
incident pathology. Prior episodes stays strong in it
(`r hr(m_rep_vague, "z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON")`), so it tracks who the
player is rather than what he did recently; and soreness is plausibly
preceded by reduced load, since a player reporting it is already being
managed, which biases its load coefficients toward null.

Reading down the `Diagnosed / control` column, only two covariates clear
the control at all. Acute load is the clear one
(`r round(hr(m_rep_named,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D") / hr(m_impact,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), 2)`x
the control), and prior injury episodes is the marginal one
(`r round(hr(m_rep_named,"z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON") / hr(m_impact,"z_PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON"), 2)`x).
The second is a modest excess, but it is in the right direction and it
is the term least explicable as court time: how often a player has
already broken down this season should not predict a jammed finger, and
it barely does. Everything else in that column sits at or below 1.0,
which is the honest reading - chronic load, in-game load two games back,
career games missed and the post-All-Star phase all predict the control
at least as strongly as they predict diagnosed overuse, so none of them
survives as a fatigue effect.

Discrimination follows the same ordering. Acute impact is lowest at
`r round(summary(m_impact)$concordance[1], 3)`, below diagnosed overuse
(`r round(summary(m_rep_named)$concordance[1], 3)`) and acute
non-contact (`r round(summary(m_load)$concordance[1], 3)`), which is
what the design predicts, though the spread is narrow enough that I
would not lean on it alone.

```{r trajectory, dependson="mechanism", fig.height=4.5, fig.width=7.5}
traj <- basehaz(m_soft, centered = FALSE) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  rename(cum_haz = hazard, game_number = time) %>%
  group_by(game_number) %>%
  summarise(cum_haz = mean(cum_haz), .groups = "drop") %>%   # average across season strata
  arrange(game_number)

haz_at <- function(g) traj$cum_haz[which.min(abs(traj$game_number - g))]

early_rate <- (haz_at(25) - haz_at(5))  / 20   # per-game hazard, games 5-25
late_rate  <- (haz_at(75) - haz_at(55)) / 20   # per-game hazard, games 55-75

fig_traj <- ggplot(traj, aes(game_number, cum_haz)) +
  geom_line(colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(title = "Baseline cumulative hazard steepens as the season progresses",
       subtitle = paste0("Per-game hazard is ", sprintf("%.2f", late_rate / early_rate),
                         "x higher in games 55-75 than in games 5-25"),
       x = "Game number within season", y = "Cumulative baseline hazard") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

fig_traj
```

## What it shows

The mechanism split is the most important result here, and it revises my
hypothesis rather than confirming it. Splitting the workload effect by
what the load could plausibly have caused separates an exposure
component, chronic load and career context, which raises the hazard of
everything including injuries load cannot cause, from a much narrower
fatigue component, acute load, which appears only on injuries fatigue
can actually produce. A pooled-outcome study reports the sum of those
two and calls it a workload effect. Separating them is the contribution,
and it is only possible because the outcome is classified on a mechanism
axis rather than as one pooled definition.

The trajectory is the clean dynamic finding. Per-game baseline hazard is
`r sprintf("%.1f", late_rate / early_rate)` x steeper in games 55–75
than games 5–25.

Note: it is a property of the baseline hazard, not of any covariate
coefficient, which is precisely why Stage 3 found no covariate drifting.
The season gets more dangerous for everyone; it does not change how
workload acts. Those are different claims and only the survival framing
separates them.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 7 - Out-of-sample validation {#stage7}

Feeds article 2.7 and 3.7.

Everything above is apparent performance, scored on the data it was
fitted to, which is optimistic by construction. `r length(coef(m3))`
covariates is ample opportunity to fit noise. Two hold-outs, chosen
because they fail differently:

-   Temporal split: train 2021-22 to 2024-25, test 2025-26. The
    operational question, and how a rolling tool would actually run.
-   Player-grouped 5-fold CV: whole players held out. A random row split
    would put LeBron's game 5 in training and game 6 in test, so the
    model could score well by memorising him.

Two safeguards: z-scores computed on training rows only, otherwise the
test distribution leaks into training; and `strata(SEASON)` dropped,
because a stratified model has no baseline for a season it never saw and
discrimination needs only the linear predictor.

```{r validation-setup, dependson="model-specs"}
zcols <- c("ROLLING_MIN_7D","ROLLING_MIN_28D","ACWR_MIN","ROLLING_GAMES_7D",
           "ROLLING_DIST_7D","ROLLING_DIST_28D","SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST","MIN",
           "PREV_GAME_MIN","PREV_2GAME_MIN",
           "ROLLING_LOAD_7D","ROLLING_LOAD_28D","ACWR_LOAD",
           "PREV_GAME_DISTANCE","PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE",
           "PREV_GAME_INTENSITY","PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY",
           "ROLLING_B2B_7D","ROLLING_B2B_28D","PLAYER_ROAD_TRIP_GAME_NUMBER",
           "TEAM_DAYS_REST","SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE","CAREER_GAMES_MISSED",
           "PRIOR_EPISODES_SEASON","PCT_THROUGH_SEASON","HEIGHT_INCHES","WEIGHT")

# primary = the reported load model; minutes = the same spec with minutes swapped in,
# validated out of sample as the robustness check (both on the new-injury outcome).
specs <- list(
  primary = list(outcome = "event", terms = c(paste0("z_", c("ROLLING_LOAD_7D","ROLLING_LOAD_28D","ROLLING_GAMES_7D","PREV_GAME_DISTANCE","PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE")),
                                              "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D","z_ROLLING_DIST_28D","z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
                                              schedule_added, context_added)),
  minutes = list(outcome = "event", terms = c(paste0("z_", c("ROLLING_MIN_7D","ROLLING_MIN_28D","ROLLING_GAMES_7D","PREV_GAME_MIN","PREV_2GAME_MIN")),
                                              "z_ROLLING_DIST_7D","z_ROLLING_DIST_28D","z_SEASON_CUMULATIVE_DIST",
                                              schedule_added, context_added))
)

# Standardise using TRAIN mean/sd only, then apply that same scaling to test.
add_z <- function(train, test, cols) {
  for (cc in cols) {
    m <- mean(train[[cc]], na.rm = TRUE); s <- sd(train[[cc]], na.rm = TRUE)
    train[[paste0("z_", cc)]] <- (train[[cc]] - m) / s
    test [[paste0("z_", cc)]] <- (test [[cc]] - m) / s
  }
  list(train = train, test = test)
}

# No season strata, so the risk score transfers to unseen seasons/players.
fit_spec <- function(data, spec) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", spec$outcome, ") ~ ",
                          paste(spec$terms, collapse = " + "), " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")),
        data = data, ties = "efron")
}

# concordance(Surv ~ x) treats larger x as LONGER survival; a Cox risk score is the
# opposite, so reverse = TRUE flips it back to the conventional C-index.
c_index <- function(fit, data, outcome) {
  d <- data
  d$.lp <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = data, type = "lp"))
  concordance(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ .lp")),
              data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance
}
```

```{r temporal-validation, dependson="validation-setup"}
test_season <- "2025-26"
tr0 <- cox %>% filter(SEASON != test_season)
te0 <- cox %>% filter(SEASON == test_season)

temporal <- map_dfr(names(specs), function(nm) {
  sp  <- specs[[nm]]
  sc  <- add_z(tr0, te0, zcols)
  fit <- fit_spec(sc$train, sp)
  tibble(model      = nm,
         apparent_C = round(c_index(fit, sc$train, sp$outcome), 4),
         temporal_C = round(c_index(fit, sc$test,  sp$outcome), 4))
})

show_tbl(temporal, paste0("Temporal validation - trained pre-", test_season,
                          ", tested on ", test_season))
```

```{r oos-calibration, dependson="temporal-validation"}
sc    <- add_z(tr0, te0, zcols)
fit_p <- fit_spec(sc$train, specs$primary)

calib_oos <- sc$test %>%
  mutate(risk = as.numeric(predict(fit_p, newdata = ., type = "lp"))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(risk)) %>%
  mutate(risk_group = ntile(risk, 5)) %>%      # 5 bands, not 10 - the test season is smaller
  group_by(risk_group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), events = sum(event),
            event_rate_1k = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 1), .groups = "drop")

show_tbl(calib_oos, "Out-of-sample calibration in the held-out season (primary model)")
```

```{r player-cv, dependson="validation-setup"}
set.seed(42)
players <- tibble(PLAYER_ID = unique(cox$PLAYER_ID),
                  fold      = sample(rep(1:5, length.out = n_distinct(cox$PLAYER_ID))))
coxf <- cox %>% left_join(players, by = "PLAYER_ID")

player_cv <- map_dfr(names(specs), function(nm) {
  sp  <- specs[[nm]]
  oos <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(coxf))          # every row gets a score from a model blind to it
  for (k in 1:5) {
    tr  <- coxf %>% filter(fold != k)       # the other four folds' players
    idx <- which(coxf$fold == k)
    sc  <- add_z(tr, coxf[idx, ], zcols)
    fit <- fit_spec(sc$train, sp)
    oos[idx] <- as.numeric(predict(fit, newdata = sc$test, type = "lp"))
  }
  d <- coxf; d$.lp <- oos
  tibble(model = nm,
         player_cv_C = round(
           concordance(as.formula(paste0("Surv(t_start, t_stop, ", sp$outcome, ") ~ .lp")),
                       data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance, 4))
})

validation_summary <- temporal %>% left_join(player_cv, by = "model")
show_tbl(validation_summary, "Validation summary - apparent vs two out-of-sample estimates")
```

## What it shows

The out-of-sample estimates land essentially on top of the apparent one.
The largest drop under either scheme is
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(validation_summary$apparent_C - validation_summary$temporal_C, validation_summary$apparent_C - validation_summary$player_cv_C))`
of concordance, and on the temporal split the held-out season actually
scores marginally higher than the training data. There is no detectable
optimism here: apparent performance is what this model would deliver on
data it has never seen. Both schemes agreeing matters, since the
temporal split would expose a model that only worked in its training
seasons and the player-grouped CV would expose one that had memorised
players.

The minutes spec lands on top of the load model out of sample, so the
exposure choice makes no difference to generalisation. Out-of-sample
calibration holds too: injury rates still climb across risk bands built
from the frozen model. The ranking transfers.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Stage 8 - Rolling risk profiles {#stage8}

Feeds article 3.7, Figure 4 and Tables 8-9. The applied deliverable.

Model 3's linear predictor is a per-player-per-game risk score, the same
quantity calibrated in Stage 3. Plotted over a season it becomes a
trajectory. To make it read as relative rather than an uninterpretable
log-hazard, I overlay the league median and IQR at each game number.
Above the band means more modelled risk than a typical player at that
point; the shape shows when.

I use Model 3 (the primary, validated model) on 2025-26 - the held-out
season, so these are genuinely prospective scores - and pick three
exemplars to span the range: LeBron James as the familiar anchor, one
player the model rates well above the league, and one it rates below.
The test is conceptual: does each profile match what we independently
know about that player's durability and availability?

```{r risk-profiles, dependson="m3", fig.height=8.5, fig.width=8}
TEST <- "2025-26"
attr(m3$terms, ".Environment") <- environment()   # see the note in the calibration chunk
cox$risk_lp <- as.numeric(predict(m3, newdata = cox, type = "lp"))
season <- cox %>% filter(SEASON == TEST, !is.na(risk_lp))

# League band: median + IQR of the risk score across everyone at each game number.
band <- season %>% group_by(game = t_stop) %>%
  summarise(q1 = quantile(risk_lp, .25), med = median(risk_lp),
            q3 = quantile(risk_lp, .75), .groups = "drop")

# Three exemplars chosen to span the risk range (see text).
# Player-level check FIRST, so the three exemplars illustrate a relationship rather
# than standing in for one. Mean risk score per player against their injury count.
player_lvl <- season %>%
  left_join(band %>% select(t_stop = game, med), by = "t_stop") %>%
  group_by(PLAYER_NAME) %>%
  summarise(intervals = n(), played = sum(PLAYED_FLAG), events = sum(event),
            missed = max(SEASON_GAMES_MISSED),
            mean_lp = mean(risk_lp), pct_above = mean(risk_lp > med), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(intervals >= 40)

rho_missed <- cor(player_lvl$mean_lp, player_lvl$missed, method = "spearman")

quint_tab <- player_lvl %>%
  mutate(q = ntile(mean_lp, 5)) %>%
  group_by(`Risk quintile` = q) %>%
  summarise(Players = n(),
            `Mean games played` = round(mean(played), 1),
            `Total injury events` = sum(events),
            `Injury events per player` = round(mean(events), 2), .groups = "drop")
rho_events <- cor(player_lvl$mean_lp, player_lvl$events, method = "spearman")
show_tbl(quint_tab, paste0("Player-level risk score against injury count, ", TEST,
                           " (Spearman rho = ", round(rho_events, 2), ")"))

# Three exemplars: two the model ranks correctly, one it does not. Chosen on injury
# EVENTS, not games missed - see the note below on why games missed is the wrong target.
picks <- tibble(
  PLAYER_NAME = c("Jalen Johnson", "LeBron James", "Jamal Shead"),
  role = c("High risk, five injury episodes - ranked correctly",
           "Average risk, three injury episodes - the model's miss",
           "Low risk, no injury episodes - ranked correctly"))

ex <- season %>% inner_join(picks, by = "PLAYER_NAME") %>%
  arrange(PLAYER_NAME, t_stop) %>% group_by(PLAYER_NAME) %>%
  mutate(seg = cumsum(c(1, as.integer(diff(t_stop) > 3)))) %>%  # break the line across absence spells
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(facet = factor(paste0(PLAYER_NAME, "\n", role),
                        levels = paste0(picks$PLAYER_NAME, "\n", picks$role)))
band_f <- tidyr::crossing(facet = levels(ex$facet), band) %>%
  mutate(facet = factor(facet, levels = levels(ex$facet)))
events <- ex %>% filter(event == 1)

# Quantitative check: does the profile match availability + injuries?
prof_tab <- season %>% inner_join(picks, by = "PLAYER_NAME") %>%
```
