  left_join(band %>% select(t_stop = game, med), by = "t_stop") %>%
  group_by(Player = PLAYER_NAME) %>%
  summarise(`Games played`  = sum(PLAYED_FLAG),
            `Injury events` = sum(event),
            `Mean risk score` = round(mean(risk_lp), 2),
            `% games above league median` = round(100 * mean(risk_lp > med)),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(`Mean risk score`))
get_stat <- function(nm, col) prof_tab[[col]][prof_tab$Player == nm]
show_tbl(prof_tab, paste0("Exemplar risk profiles vs actual availability, ", TEST))

fig_profiles <- ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = band_f, aes(game, ymin = q1, ymax = q3), fill = "grey80", alpha = .6) +
  geom_line(data = band_f, aes(game, med), colour = "grey45", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(data = ex, aes(t_stop, risk_lp, group = seg, colour = facet), linewidth = .8) +
  geom_point(data = ex, aes(t_stop, risk_lp, colour = facet), size = .9) +
  geom_point(data = events, aes(t_stop, risk_lp), shape = 4, size = 3, stroke = 1.1,
             colour = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~ facet, ncol = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#b2182b", "#2166ac", "#1a9850"), guide = "none") +
  labs(title = paste0("Rolling injury-risk profiles, ", TEST),
       subtitle = "Model 3 risk score by game. Grey = league IQR, dashed = league median, red x = injury onset.",
       x = "Game number within season", y = "Risk score (Model 3 linear predictor)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))
fig_profiles
```

## What it shows

The quintile table is the general claim: player-level mean risk score
orders injury count across the season (Spearman rho =
`r round(rho_events, 2)`), so the three profiles illustrate a real
relationship rather than standing in for one.

Two of three line up. Jalen Johnson sits above the IQR essentially all
season (`r get_stat("Jalen Johnson", "% games above league median")`%)
with `r get_stat("Jalen Johnson", "Injury events")` onsets, the season's
highest burden. Jamal Shead runs along the bottom unbroken with none.
LeBron James is the miss: average-risk read,
`r get_stat("LeBron James", "Injury events")` onsets. At concordance
`r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 2)` about one pair in three is
ordered wrongly, so a three-player figure has no right to be immune.

A note on what these profiles are scored against. The instinct is to
validate against games missed, and that is the wrong target. Across the
`r nrow(player_lvl)` players with 40+ modelled intervals in `r TEST`,
mean risk score correlates with games missed at Spearman
`r round(rho_missed, 2)`, negative: higher-scoring players miss fewer
games, because a high score requires high load and high load requires
being available. Games missed mixes injury with rest, load management
and coaching decisions. Onsets are what the model is fitted to.

Two caveats. The score is relative, so it ranks but gives no absolute
probability. And even Shead, low-risk , sits only modestly below the
median, which is the health-selection wall made visual: you cannot post
a very low load-based score and play a full season, because availability
is what drives the load the score is built from. The lowest scores in
the league belong to players barely in the rotation.

The why lives in the same object. The score is a weighted sum, so a
player's elevation on any game decomposes into how much comes from acute
load, congestion or injury history, which is the per-player readout a
practitioner would act on.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Conclusion

Where I got to, and what carries into the article.

1.  The mechanism split decomposes workload into exposure and fatigue.
    Chronic load predicts every tier at similar strength, and returns
    its *lowest* value on diagnosed overuse
    (`r hr(m_rep_named, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")`) against
    `r hr(m_impact, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` on injuries it cannot
    possibly cause. That ordering is backwards for a fatigue mechanism
    and exactly right for an exposure measure, and for a contact injury
    exposure *is* the causal route. Acute load is the covariate that
    tells the tiers apart, and only once chronic load is held fixed,
    which is what turns it from a volume proxy into a measure of how
    recently that volume arrived. Both components are real and no
    pooled-outcome study can separate them. That separation is the
    contribution.

2.  The fatigue signal is acute load, and it is **specific rather than
    small**. It is the largest effect in the analysis on diagnosed
    overuse (`r hr(m_rep_named, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`, p =
    `r fmt_p(summary(m_rep_named)$coefficients["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "Pr(>|z|)"])`)
    and on acute non-contact injury
    (`r hr(m_load, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`), and indistinguishable from no
    effect on the control (`r hr(m_impact, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`, p =
    `r fmt_p(summary(m_impact)$coefficients["z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "Pr(>|z|)"])`).
    Size and significance agree, which is what makes it read as
    specificity rather than noise. This is not the monotone fade across
    tiers I expected and reported earlier; it is sharper than that.

3.  The load-overuse relationship is only visible when the outcome is a
    **diagnosed pathology**. Where a pathology is named, acute load is
    `r hr(m_rep_named, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`. Where the report says only
    that something is sore, it is
    `r hr(m_rep_vague, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` on
    `r format(sum(cox$ev_rep_vague), big.mark = ",")` events, a
    well-powered null rather than a thin one. Pooling them hides both.
    That is a finding about measurement as much as physiology: injury
    surveillance built on availability text will understate the workload
    effect on overuse injury, because most of what such data records as
    overuse is not a diagnosis.

4.  Prior injury is the largest change in a player's risk profile, and
    the covariates do not carry it. Holding workload, schedule and
    context equal, a player in their second injury spell of a season
    carries `r esc2`x the baseline hazard of a player in their first and
    a third-or-later spell `r esc3`x. Because the spell strata take no
    coefficient, none of that is attributable to load; it sits in the
    baseline, where no amount of load management would show it.

5.  Load is interchangeable with minutes, and catching why mattered. I
    report load as the better construct, and the model holds identically
    on minutes. An earlier version had load out-predicting minutes for
    soft tissue (0.693 → 0.744); that was a tracking-data bug, DNP games
    leaking a fake zero distance through the carry-forward, not a real
    edge. Distance is the right idea, but in public data total load ≈
    minutes (r ≈ 0.99) and the injurious high-speed component is
    unobserved.

6.  The season's danger is in the baseline, not the coefficients.
    Baseline hazard `r sprintf("%.1f", late_rate / early_rate)`x steeper
    late season while covariate effects stay proportional. Heavy chronic
    load is equally bad in October and April; the background rises.

7.  Proneness is real, and the covariates absorb two thirds of it. θ =
    `r round(theta, 3)` against `r round(theta_steps[1], 3)` unadjusted,
    so the 90th-to-10th spread narrows from
    `r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps[1])), 1)`x to
    `r round(exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sd_frail), 1)`x. What remains is the
    reach of public data.

## Limitations

-   Health-gating is not solved. Point-in-time rest and back-to-back
    covariates read protective because coaches rest at-risk players. I
    mark them rather than interpret them; observational data cannot
    remove the bias.
-   The outcome is availability, not diagnosis. "Listed Out with a
    reason", not a clinician's assessment, and the reason text is
    inconsistent.
-   Concordance `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(m3)$concordance[1])` to
    `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(m3_ag)$concordance[1])` is the
    public-data ceiling. No GPS, no medical screening, no training load.
    Better framed as establishing that ceiling than as a competitive
    predictor.
-   The lagged terms cost coverage. First two appearances each season
    cannot be scored, so the model fits
    `r format(m3$nevent, big.mark = ",")` of
    `r format(sum(cox$event), big.mark = ",")` events. Early-season
    injury is the blind spot, and a fair price for a correctly-signed
    prospective term.
-   The deep bench adds uninformative at-risk time, but excluding on
    this season's games played would condition on the outcome.
-   Intensity is a per-game distance-per-minute average, which cannot
    resolve high-speed and acceleration efforts. Its null is evidence
    about this measure, not the construct.
-   Mechanism tiers involve judgement. Regex on free text; defensible
    but not uniquely so.
-   Five seasons, one league, two COVID-affected.

# Appendix - Robustness and sensitivity checks {#appendix}

Checks that the headline result does not depend on a modelling choice I
made. Each re-fits the reported specification with one decision changed
and reports what moves. They sit here rather than in the main sequence
because none of them changes a conclusion; the point of each is that
nothing happens.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Does the exposure choice matter?

Load and minutes are \~`r round(r_load_min, 3)` collinear, so does the
choice matter? Refitting Model 3 with minutes swapped in leaves
discrimination and the headline hazard ratios essentially unchanged.

```{r robustness-minutes, dependson="model-specs"}
m3_min <- fit_cox(m3_terms_min)   # same Model 3, minutes in place of load

robust_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Concordance", "Chronic workload HR (per SD)",
             "Acute workload HR (per SD)"),
  `Load (reported)` = c(
    round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
    hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
  `Minutes (robustness)` = c(
    round(summary(m3_min)$concordance[1], 4),
    hr(m3_min, "z_ROLLING_MIN_28D"), hr(m3_min, "z_ROLLING_MIN_7D"))
)
show_tbl(robust_tab, "Robustness - on-court load vs minutes give the same answer")
```

So the exposure choice is not driving the result. I lead with load
because it is the better construct, what the body absorbed rather than
what the coach decided.

## Is the 2-games-back term its own signal?

Lag-2 carries correctly-signed load effect in the model. Two ways it
could be an illusion: it might just be re-expressing the 7d/28d rolling
windows, or its contribution might be in-sample overfitting.

```{r sensitivity-lag2, dependson="model-specs"}
load_block <- c("z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D", "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")

# How much of lag-2 do the rolling windows explain? VIF < 5 = estimable alongside them.
lag2_vif <- 1 / (1 - summary(lm(z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE ~ z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D +
                   z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D, data = cox))$r.squared)

# Out of sample: refit on 2021-25, score the unseen 2025-26, with and without lag-2.
tr <- cox %>% filter(SEASON != "2025-26"); te <- cox %>% filter(SEASON == "2025-26")
oos_c <- function(terms) {           # no season strata, so the score transfers
  f <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(terms, collapse = " + "),
                               " + cluster(PLAYER_ID)")), data = tr, ties = "efron")
  d <- te; d$.lp <- as.numeric(predict(f, newdata = te, type = "lp"))
  round(concordance(Surv(t_start, t_stop, event) ~ .lp, data = d, reverse = TRUE)$concordance, 4)
}

oos_with <- oos_c(m3_terms)
oos_less <- oos_c(setdiff(m3_terms, "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE"))

lag2_tab <- tibble(
  Check = c("VIF of lag-2 against the rolling-load block",
            "Out-of-sample C, lag-2 in the model",
            "Out-of-sample C, lag-2 dropped"),
  Value = c(round(lag2_vif, 2),
            oos_with, oos_less))
show_tbl(lag2_tab, "Is the 2-games-back term its own signal?")
```

VIF is inside the conventional threshold of 5, so lag-2 is estimable
alongside the rolling windows. I

What justifies keeping it is the hold-out: concordance `r oos_with` with
lag-2 against `r oos_less` without. It adds predictive value on a season
the model never saw, which is the test that matters for a term I report
as a finding.

## Does intensity add anything beyond volume?

Load and minutes are both volume. Intensity is the obvious candidate for
what they miss: how hard, not how long. It is nearly uncorrelated with
the load terms, so if it carried independent signal this is where it
would show. I add the same prospective lag pair to Model 3 and test
whether both terms are jointly zero.

```{r robustness-intensity, dependson="model-specs"}
# Fit on the rows where intensity is defined for BOTH models, so the comparison is like for like (intensity needs >=10 minutes played, so it is missing more often than load).
need_int <- c(setdiff(m3_terms, "I(z_SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE^2)"), intensity_terms)
cox_int  <- cox %>% filter(if_all(all_of(need_int), ~ !is.na(.)))

m3_int_base <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
                     " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox_int, ties = "efron")
m3_int_plus <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ",
                     paste(c(m3_terms, intensity_terms), collapse = " + "),
                     " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox_int, ties = "efron")

# Joint robust Wald test that both intensity coefficients are zero.
cf <- coef(m3_int_plus); V <- vcov(m3_int_plus); idx <- match(intensity_terms, names(cf))
int_wald <- as.numeric(t(cf[idx]) %*% solve(V[idx, idx]) %*% cf[idx])
int_p    <- pchisq(int_wald, length(idx), lower.tail = FALSE)

intensity_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Concordance", "Chronic load HR (per SD)", "Acute load HR (per SD)",
             "In-game intensity, last game (per SD)", "In-game intensity, 2 games back (per SD)"),
  `Model 3` = c(round(summary(m3_int_base)$concordance[1], 4),
                hr(m3_int_base, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_int_base, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"), NA, NA),
  `+ intensity` = c(round(summary(m3_int_plus)$concordance[1], 4),
                hr(m3_int_plus, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_int_plus, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
                hr(m3_int_plus, "z_PREV_GAME_INTENSITY"), hr(m3_int_plus, "z_PREV_2GAME_INTENSITY"))
)
show_tbl(intensity_tab, paste0("Intensity robustness - joint Wald test that both intensity terms are zero: p = ",
                               fmt_p(int_p)))
```

Intensity adds nothing once volume is accounted for. Concordance
unchanged to three decimals, load hazard ratios unmoved, both intensity
terms close to 1.

These players all move at broadly similar rates, so a per-SD move in
intensity is a small physical change. This is evidence that the narrow
band of intensity visible in public tracking data carries no signal
beyond volume, not that effort is irrelevant. The high-speed and
acceleration component the literature implicates is not resolvable in a
per-game distance-per-minute average. Intensity stays out of the primary
model.

## Does the deep bench dilute the result?

The sample is every player who appeared at all, including the very end
of the rotation: 1-to-20-game seasons, single-digit minutes. Their
availability is driven by roster politics more than health, so they add
at-risk time that is largely noise. About 23% of player-seasons and 11%
of rows, but under 5% of events, which is the profile of observations
that dilute rather than inform.

A player appears in few games precisely because he got hurt, so
filtering on current availability deletes the injured and biases the
effect toward null. That is conditioning on a post-baseline outcome.
Instead the cohort is defined ex ante on the previous season's minutes
per game, fixed before any of this season's injuries.

```{r sensitivity-rotation, dependson="model-specs"}
ROTATION_MPG <- 15   # prior-season minutes per game: an established rotation player

rot_groups <- cox %>%
  mutate(Group = case_when(
    is.na(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG)              ~ "No prior-season record",
    PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG >= ROTATION_MPG     ~ paste0("Rotation (>= ", ROTATION_MPG, " mpg)"),
    TRUE                                    ~ paste0("Below threshold (< ", ROTATION_MPG, " mpg)"))) %>%
  group_by(Group) %>%
  summarise(`Intervals` = n(), Events = sum(event),
            `Events per 1,000 intervals` = round(1000 * sum(event) / n(), 2), .groups = "drop")
show_tbl(rot_groups, "Event rate by prior-season role (the dilution, quantified)")

rate_of  <- function(pat) rot_groups[["Events per 1,000 intervals"]][grepl(pat, rot_groups$Group)]
rate_low <- rate_of("Below"); rate_rot <- rate_of("Rotation"); rate_na <- rate_of("No prior")
n_noprior <- cox %>% distinct(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(is.na(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG))) %>% pull(n)

# season's injuries occur and the cohort stays ex ante.
cox <- cox %>%
  mutate(CAREER_MPG     = if_else(CAREER_GAMES > 0, CAREER_MINUTES / CAREER_GAMES, NA_real_),
         ROTATION_BASIS = coalesce(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG, CAREER_MPG))

n_restored <- cox %>% distinct(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(is.na(PRIOR_SEASON_MIN_PG) & ROTATION_BASIS >= ROTATION_MPG, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  pull(n)

cox_rot <- cox %>% filter(ROTATION_BASIS >= ROTATION_MPG)
m3_rot  <- coxph(as.formula(paste0(surv_lhs, " ~ ", paste(m3_terms, collapse = " + "),
                 " + ", rhs_tail)), data = cox_rot, ties = "efron")

rot_tab <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Player-intervals (n)", "Events", "Concordance",
             "Chronic load HR (per SD)", "Acute load HR (per SD)",
             "In-game load, last game", "In-game load, 2 games back"),
  `All players (primary)` = c(m3$n, m3$nevent, round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
     hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
     hr(m3, "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE"), hr(m3, "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE")),
  `Rotation players only` = c(m3_rot$n, m3_rot$nevent, round(summary(m3_rot)$concordance[1], 4),
     hr(m3_rot, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_rot, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
     hr(m3_rot, "z_PREV_GAME_DISTANCE"), hr(m3_rot, "z_PREV_2GAME_DISTANCE"))
)
show_tbl(rot_tab, paste0("Sensitivity - restricted to established rotation players (>= ",
                         ROTATION_MPG, " mpg in the prior season, or across their career ",
                         "where the prior season is missing)"))
```

The workload result is not an artefact of the deep bench. Restricting to
established rotation players raises the workload hazard ratios.
Discrimination goes the other way.

A more homogeneous cohort estimates the effects on a cleaner population
while leaving less variation to rank. Full sample stays primary because
it describes the league, not a subset.

Filtering on prior-season minutes alone silently deletes the
`r n_noprior` player-seasons with no prior-season record, because `NA`
fails a `>=` test. The group is Klay Thompson, Kawhi Leonard, Jamal
Murray, John Wall, Zion Williamson, all of whom missed a full season
through injury. Dropping the highest injury-burden players in the league
on a this would bias the check in the one direction . Where the prior
season is missing I fall back to career minutes per game, restoring
`r n_restored` player-seasons. Career totals use only seasons before the
modelled one, so the cohort stays ex ante.

I keep the full sample as primary (it is the honest population of NBA
players and the broader claim) Rookies sit outside this check by
construction: no prior season, no career history to fall back on.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Does the choice of time scale matter?

Everything above runs on one time axis: the player's position through
their team's scheduled games. That is a modelling decision, not a fact
about the data, and it usually goes unexamined. So I tested the
alternative.

The competing clock counts a player's at-risk intervals, closing the
gaps injury absences leave. LeBron's first 2025-26 appearance is game 15
on the scheduled clock and game 1 on this one. Not cosmetic: it changes
who sits in the same risk set. Scheduled compares players at the same
point in the season, at-risk compares them at the same number of
available games.

```{r clock-robustness, dependson=c("m3","mechanism")}
cox_b <- cox %>% arrange(SEASON, PLAYER_ID, t_stop) %>%
  group_by(SEASON, PLAYER_ID) %>%
  mutate(b_stop = row_number(), b_start = b_stop - 1L) %>% ungroup()
stopifnot(all(cox_b$b_stop > cox_b$b_start))

fit_b <- function(outcome, terms = m3_terms) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(b_start, b_stop, ", outcome, ") ~ ",
        paste(terms, collapse = " + "), " + ", rhs_tail)),
        data = cox_b, ties = "efron")
}
m3_b     <- fit_b("event")
msoft_b  <- fit_b("event_repetitive"); mload_b <- fit_b("event_acute_nc")
mimp_b   <- fit_b("event_acute_imp")

clock_tab <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("Model 3: chronic load (28d)", "Model 3: acute load (7d)",
               "Model 3: concordance",
               "Repetitive: chronic / acute", "Acute non-contact: chronic / acute",
               "Acute impact: chronic / acute"),
  `Scheduled-game clock` = c(
    hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
    round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4),
    paste(hr(m_soft,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  "/", hr(m_soft,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(m_load,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  "/", hr(m_load,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(m_impact,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),"/", hr(m_impact,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"))),
  `At-risk-interval clock` = c(
    hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"),
    round(summary(m3_b)$concordance[1], 4),
    paste(hr(msoft_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), "/", hr(msoft_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(mload_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), "/", hr(mload_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
    paste(hr(mimp_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  "/", hr(mimp_b,"z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"))))

# How far apart are the two clocks in the first place?
clock_gap <- cox_b %>% summarise(
  `Rows where the clocks agree` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100*mean(t_stop == b_stop)),
  `Mean absolute difference`    = round(mean(abs(t_stop - b_stop)), 2),
  `Largest difference`          = max(abs(t_stop - b_stop)))

show_tbl(clock_tab, "Time-scale robustness: scheduled-game clock vs at-risk-interval clock")
show_tbl(clock_gap, "How far apart the two clocks actually are")
```

## What it shows

Nothing moves. Chronic load `r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")` to
`r hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D")`, acute load
`r hr(m3, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` to `r hr(m3_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")`,
concordance `r round(summary(m3)$concordance[1], 4)` to
`r round(summary(m3_b)$concordance[1], 4)`. The mechanism split holds:
acute load still collapses to `r hr(mimp_b, "z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")` in the
control.

I had expected chronic load to fall, on the reasoning that a clock
counting available games would absorb some of the exposure signal. It
does not. The clocks agree on
`r clock_gap[["Rows where the clocks agree"]]` of rows and differ by
`r clock_gap[["Mean absolute difference"]]` games on average, so
absences are not frequent enough to reshape the risk sets. Season
progress moves, but that is redistribution.

Scheduled clock stays primary. It is the axis where the baseline hazard
has a season interpretation (Stage 6), and the one that puts players
available on the same night in the same risk set, which is the
comparison a team makes. The estimates do not depend on it, which is the
useful part.

# Article export {.unnumbered}

Everything the journal article uses is written out from here, so the
article can never drift from this report. Figures go to `docs/figures/`
at print resolution, tables to `docs/tables/` as CSV. Re-knitting
regenerates all of them.

```{r article-export, dependson=c("risk-set-schematic","calibration-plot","trajectory","risk-profiles","hr-table","recurrent-compare","mechanism","player-cv","sensitivity-rotation","robustness-intensity","robustness-minutes","ph-decomp","stage0-screening","nested-tests","oos-calibration","ag-model")}
FIG <- here("docs", "figures"); TAB <- here("docs", "tables")
dir.create(FIG, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
dir.create(TAB, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

# Print styling: larger base type than the screen version, because these land in a
# Word document at roughly half the on-screen width.
print_theme <- theme(text = element_text(size = 13),
                     plot.title = element_blank(),      # the article caption carries the title
                     plot.subtitle = element_blank())

save_fig <- function(plot, name, w, h) {
  ggsave(file.path(FIG, paste0(name, ".png")), plot + print_theme,
         width = w, height = h, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
  invisible(name)
}

save_fig(fig_riskset,  "figure1_risk_set_schematic", 10.0, 4.6)
save_fig(fig_calib,    "figure2_calibration_decile",  7.0, 4.5)
save_fig(fig_traj,     "figure3_baseline_hazard",     7.5, 4.5)
save_fig(fig_profiles, "figure4_rolling_profiles",    8.0, 8.5)

# Appendix B1: all 25 scaled-Schoenfeld curves on one sheet. cox.zph plots are base
# graphics, so this is drawn straight to a device rather than through ggsave.
png(file.path(FIG, "appendixB1_schoenfeld_panel.png"),
    width = 10, height = 12.5, units = "in", res = 200)
op <- par(mfrow = c(7, 4), mar = c(3.4, 3.6, 2.0, 0.8), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0), cex = 0.62)
for (v in plot_terms) {
  idx <- which(rownames(zph3$table) == v)
  plot(zph3[idx], resid = FALSE, lwd = 1.6, col = "steelblue",

}

# Tables. Each is written exactly as the article reports it, so the article can be

# Presentation export {.unnumbered}

Slide versions of the figures: fewer elements, much larger type, and one
new figure that the article does not need. The negative control is a
table in the article, but it is the centre of the talk, so it gets a
purpose-built chart here. Everything writes to
`docs/figures/presentation/`.

```{r presentation-export, dependson=c("mechanism","calibration-plot","trajectory","risk-profiles","frailty-nested","risk-set-schematic")}
PFIG <- here("docs", "figures", "presentation")
dir.create(PFIG, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

pres_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 19) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 21),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 15, colour = "grey30"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 16),
        legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 15))

psave <- function(pl, name, w = 11, h = 6.2)
  ggsave(file.path(PFIG, paste0(name, ".png")), pl, width = w, height = h,
         dpi = 200, bg = "white")

## P1 - the money figure, on the four-tier split. Chronic load is flat across the
## tiers and largest in the CONTROL; acute load spikes where a pathology is actually
## named and collapses everywhere else. That contrast IS the decomposition argument.
## Point estimates are plotted, significance is marked, because the argument needs both.
tier_lv <- c("Overuse\n(diagnosed)", "Overuse\n(symptom only)",
             "Acute\nnon-contact", "Acute impact\n(CONTROL)")
p1_mods <- list(m_rep_named, m_rep_vague, m_load, m_impact)

pull_hr <- function(term) map_dbl(p1_mods, ~ hr(.x, term))
pull_p  <- function(term) map_dbl(p1_mods, ~ summary(.x)$coefficients[term, "Pr(>|z|)"])

neg <- tibble(
  tier = factor(rep(tier_lv, 2), levels = tier_lv),
  what = rep(c("Chronic load (28d)", "Acute load (7d)"), each = 4),
  hr   = c(pull_hr("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"), pull_hr("z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D")),
  p    = c(pull_p("z_ROLLING_LOAD_28D"),  pull_p("z_ROLLING_LOAD_7D"))) %>%
  mutate(sig   = p < 0.05,
         # label carries the estimate; "ns" flags the ones you cannot distinguish from 1
         label = ifelse(sig, sprintf("%.2f", hr), sprintf("%.2f\nns", hr)))

p_neg <- ggplot(neg, aes(tier, hr, colour = what, group = what)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55", linewidth = .7) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.6) +
  # hollow points = not distinguishable from no effect, solid = significant
  geom_point(aes(shape = sig, fill = what), size = 5.5, stroke = 1.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), vjust = -0.85, size = 5.2, fontface = "bold",
            lineheight = .85, show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("segment", x = 3.55, xend = 3.9, y = 2.42, yend = 2.42,
           colour = "grey35", linewidth = .5) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.72, y = 2.62, label = "load cannot cause these",
           size = 4.6, colour = "grey25", fontface = "italic") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 21, `FALSE` = 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Chronic load (28d)" = "#2166AC", "Acute load (7d)" = "#B2182B")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Chronic load (28d)" = "#2166AC", "Acute load (7d)" = "#B2182B"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.75, 2.85), breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2, 2.5)) +
  labs(title = "Load cannot cause a jammed finger, but it predicts one",
       subtitle = paste("Hazard ratio per SD; hollow points are not significant.",
                        "Chronic load is largest in the control.",
                        "Acute load only bites where a pathology is named."),
       x = NULL, y = "Hazard ratio") +
  pres_theme
psave(p_neg, "P1_negative_control")

## P2 - calibration, simplified
p_cal <- ggplot(calib, aes(risk_group, event_rate_1k)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2166AC", width = .68) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(event_rate_1k)), vjust = -0.5, size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .12))) +
  labs(title = "Higher risk score, more injuries",
       subtitle = "Observed injury rate by predicted-risk decile. Every step rises.",
       x = "Risk decile (1 = lowest)", y = "Injuries per 1,000 games") +
  pres_theme
psave(p_cal, "P2_calibration")

## P3 - baseline hazard, simplified
p_traj <- ggplot(traj, aes(game_number, cum_haz)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#B2182B", linewidth = 1.7) +
  labs(title = "The season itself gets more dangerous",
       subtitle = sprintf("Per-game baseline hazard is %.1fx steeper late season, for an average player",
                          late_rate / early_rate),
       x = "Game number", y = "Cumulative baseline hazard") +
  pres_theme
psave(p_traj, "P3_baseline_hazard")

## P4 - frailty progression: the spread the covariates absorb
fr <- tibble(step = factor(c("No covariates", "+ Workload", "+ Schedule", "+ Player context"),
                           levels = c("No covariates", "+ Workload", "+ Schedule", "+ Player context")),
             spread = exp(2 * qnorm(0.9) * sqrt(theta_steps)))
p_fr <- ggplot(fr, aes(step, spread)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2166AC", width = .66) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1fx", spread)), vjust = -0.45, size = 6, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .15))) +
  labs(title = "The model explains two thirds of what separates players",
       subtitle = "Spread in injury proneness, 90th vs 10th percentile, as covariates are added",
       x = NULL, y = "Hazard spread") +
  pres_theme
psave(p_fr, "P4_frailty_progression")

## P5 - rolling profiles, larger type
psave(fig_profiles + theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
        theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0, size = 14),
              plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 20)),
      "P5_rolling_profiles", w = 10.5, h = 7.4)

## P6 - risk-set schematic, larger type
psave(fig_riskset + theme(text = element_text(size = 15),
                          legend.text = element_text(size = 12)),
      "P6_risk_set", w = 12, h = 5.6)

tibble(File = list.files(PFIG, pattern = "\\.png$")) %>%
  show_tbl("Slide figures written")
```

# References {.unnumbered}

Compiled for review: verify each entry's details before the final
reference list. Grouped by role, with a note on where each is used.

Statistical methodology

1.  Therneau TM, Grambsch PM. Modeling Survival Data: Extending the Cox
    Model. New York: Springer; 2000. The counting-process Cox framework
    and time-varying covariates (whole pipeline).
2.  Andersen PK, Gill RD. Cox's regression model for counting processes:
    a large sample study. Annals of Statistics. 1982;10(4):1100–1120.
    The Andersen–Gill recurrent-events model (Stage 4).
3.  Prentice RL, Williams BJ, Peterson AV. On the regression analysis of
    multivariate failure time data. Biometrika. 1981;68(2):373–379. The
    PWP gap-time model (Stage 4).
4.  Grambsch PM, Therneau TM. Proportional hazards tests and diagnostics
    based on weighted residuals. Biometrika. 1994;81(3):515–526. The
    scaled-Schoenfeld PH test behind `cox.zph` (Stage 2).
5.  Harrell FE Jr, Califf RM, Pryor DB, Lee KL, Rosati RA. Evaluating
    the yield of medical tests. JAMA. 1982;247(18):2543–2546. The
    concordance index (Harrell's C), used throughout for discrimination.
6.  Lipsitch M, Tchetgen Tchetgen E, Cohen T. Negative controls: a tool
    for detecting confounding and bias in observational studies.
    Epidemiology. 2010;21(3):383-388. The framework for the Stage 5
    mechanism split: the definition of a negative-control outcome, the
    conditions under which one is informative, and the reading that a
    control which fires has detected confounding rather than failed.
7.  Efron B. The efficiency of Cox's likelihood function for censored
    data. Journal of the American Statistical Association.
    1977;72(359):557–565. The Efron approximation for tied event times
    (`ties = "efron"`).

Injury classification and outcome definition

8.  Bahr R, Clarsen B, Derman W, et al. International Olympic Committee
    consensus statement: methods for recording and reporting of
    epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport 2020 (including
    the STROBE Extension for Sport Injury and Illness Surveillance,
    STROBE-SIIS). British Journal of Sports Medicine.
    2020;54(7):372-389. The framework for classifying injuries on
    independent axes (body region, tissue type, mechanism, severity),
    the acute / repetitive / mixed mechanism categories behind the Stage
    5 tiers, and the time-loss severity bands.
9.  Toohey LA, Drew MK, Fortington LV, Finch CF, Cook JL. An updated
    subsequent injury categorisation model (SIC-2.0): data-driven
    categorisation of subsequent injuries in sport. Sports Medicine.
    2018;48(9):2199-2210. The data-driven categories used to classify
    subsequent injuries on site, nature and side with no clinical input,
    which is why this model rather than a recovery-based definition.
10. Finch CF, Cook J. Categorising sports injuries in epidemiological
    studies: the subsequent injury categorisation (SIC) model to address
    multiple, recurrent and exacerbation of injuries. British Journal of
    Sports Medicine. 2014;48(17):1276-1280. The original SIC model that
    SIC-2.0 extends.
11. Fuller CW, Ekstrand J, Junge A, et al. Consensus statement on injury
    definitions and data collection procedures in studies of football
    (soccer) injuries. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in
    Sports. 2006;16(2):83-92. The basis for counting a same-site injury
    after a return to play as a recurrent injury rather than a
    continuation of the previous one, which is why my rule merges only
    repeats arriving before a durable return.
12. Heiderscheit BC, Sherry MA, Silder A, Chumanov ES, Thelen DG.
    Hamstring strain injuries: recommendations for diagnosis,
    rehabilitation, and injury prevention. Journal of Orthopaedic &
    Sports Physical Therapy. 2010;40(2):67-81. Source of the roughly
    two-week post-return window used to set the durability threshold:
    about a third of hamstring injuries recur, with the greatest risk in
    the initial two weeks after return to sport, attributed to
    inadequate rehabilitation or a premature return.
13. Eftekhari A, Cogan C, Pandya N, Feeley B. Hamstring injury
    epidemiology in the National Basketball Association over a five-year
    period. Muscles, Ligaments and Tendons Journal. 2022;12(2).
    Basketball-specific evidence on repeat injury: 81.4% of NBA players
    with a hamstring injury sustained a subsequent injury in the same
    and/or following season, and those repeats are counted as subsequent
    injuries rather than merged.
14. Green B, Schache AG, Pizzari T. What is a recurrence? The onset,
    frequency and time loss impact of recurrent calf muscle strain
    injuries in elite male Australian football players over a decade.
    BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2025;11(3):e002865. Applies the
    IOC recurrence/exacerbation distinction to a decade of surveillance
    data and documents how much subsequent-injury definitions vary
    between studies.
15. Orchard JW, Meeuwisse W, Derman W, et al. Sport Medicine Diagnostic
    Coding System (SMDCS) and the Orchard Sports Injury and Illness
    Classification System (OSIICS): revised 2020 consensus versions.
    British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020;54(7):397-401. The coding
    systems that operationalise the IOC axes as body-part plus pathology
    codes; my parsed site and tissue fields follow the same split.

Applied / domain

16. Russell JL, McLean BD, Impellizzeri FM, Strack DS, Coutts AJ.
    Measuring physical demands in basketball: an explorative systematic
    review of practices. Sports Medicine. 2021;51(1):81–112. Justifies
    the on-court external-load (tracking-distance) exposure. (A review
    of load-monitoring methods; it does not support an experience/tenure
    inverted-U, so it is no longer cited for the `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE²`
    term.)
17. Chan C-C, Yung PS-H, Mok K-M. The relationship between training load
    and injury risk in basketball: a systematic review. Healthcare.
    2024;12(18):1829. The training-load–injury evidence base, including
    U-shaped load–risk findings (motivates the load block).
18. Martin [author initials / journal to verify] et al. Rookie-season
    injury and career longevity in NBA players. 2021. Durability /
    injury-proneness (frailty stage, and the durability side of the
    `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE²` term).
19. Hägglund M, Waldén M, Ekstrand J. Previous injury as a risk factor
    for injury in elite football: a prospective study over two
    consecutive seasons. British Journal of Sports Medicine.
    2006;40(9):767–772. Prior injury as a risk factor (the prior-episode
    and recent-return covariates).

Tenure / age: the non-linear `SEASONS_IN_LEAGUE²` term

20. National Basketball Association. Player Participation Policy.
    Approved by the NBA Board of Governors, September 2023. The
    institutional mechanism: pre-approved back-to-back rest for players
    aged 35+, or with roughly 34,000 career regular-season minutes or
    1,000 career games, or a serious injury history. Younger players
    receive no equivalent allowance, so acute load differs
    systematically by tenure. (Formalised from 2023-24; the same
    veteran-rest pattern existed informally earlier in the study window.
    Note the CBA's "Years of Service" provisions govern contracts and
    salary, not rest, so the Participation Policy, not the CBA, is the
    correct citation here.)
21. Morikawa LH, Tummala SV, Brinkman JC, Buckner Petty SA, Chhabra A.
    Effect of a condensed NBA season on injury risk: an analysis of the
    2020 season and player safety. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports
    Medicine. 2022;10(9). Older players showed disproportionately larger
    injury increases under schedule compression.
22. Drakos MC, Domb B, Starkey C, Callahan L, Allen AA. Injury in the
    National Basketball Association: a 17-year overview. Sports Health.
    2010;2(4):284–290. Early NBA epidemiology found no clean linear
    age-injury association, supporting a non-linear specification.
